items.descriptionOriginal: In the early 2000s, The Beatles ‘ hits were considered oldies and mostly played on throwback radio stations. Today? They’re another twenty years older. It’s easy to see The Beatles like the faces on Mount Rushmore: iconic and historically important, but no longer relevant. What many people miss is the timeless quality of The Beatles’ songwriting . While the sound and production of their music hark back to a bygone era, the lyrics and emotion could never go out of style. Sometimes it just takes listening in a new way to hear it. Artist covers The Beatles in a modern rock style Alex Melton is a popular musician and content creator with over 510,000 subscribers on his YouTube channel. He’s built a rabid following with wildly creative covers, often putting a pop-punk or 2000s spin on everything from pop to country to even a few oldies. He recently dug up a classic Beatles tune, “Don’t Let Me Down,” and reimagined it for the 21st century. He brings it to life in his very own way with electric guitar, sweet drum fills, and surprise key changes. The result is reminiscent of Switchfoot, Finger Eleven, Foo Fighters, and many other influential 2000s rock bands. It’s a must-listen. Listeners and viewers are clamoring for the full album Originally released on the B-side of The Beatles’ hit single “Get Back,” “Don’t Let Me Down” is a cult favorite. Melton’s electrifying cover is sparking nostalgia among Beatles fans and maybe even wooing some new ones. Commenters flooded Melton’s video with praise: “Now we need a Beatles covers album” “So stoked for this one!! More Beatles pls!!” “As a 35 year old who also just got into the Beatles and watched Get Back, I am SO here for this. Don’t Let Me Down and I’ve Got A Feeling are two of my favorites from them.” “Oh boy, I could use a whole EP of these!” “This is how you can tell that doing a cover is an art of its own. This echoes of the original in a way that feels instantly familiar and yet entirely brand new. This is how you cover a Beatles song.” “It’s never too late to get into a Beatles phase, more power to ya!” Melton writes in his YouTube channel description that, at 36, he never had much interest in The Beatles beyond a distant appreciation for their musical contributions. But the 2021 documentary Get Back , directed by Peter Jackson, sucked him in. “The four guys were so compelling and charming and funny and not afraid to be artists,” he writes. “So now I’m in my Beatles phase, at 36 years old.” Sometimes a new spin and a fresh interpretation are exactly what a new audience needs to appreciate the brilliance of the original more deeply. The post Artist reimagines the Beatles’ ‘Don’t Let Me Down’ as a modern rock song and people are demanding a full album appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένας καθηγητής ρώτησε τους μαθητές πού έσωσαν την εργασία τους. Κάποιοι δεν κατάλαβαν την ερώτηση.
items.titleOriginal: A professor asked students where they saved their work. Some didn’t understand the question.
items.description: Η καθηγήτρια μηχανικής Catherine Garland ρώτησε τους μαθητές της πού είχαν αποθηκεύσει τα αρχεία του υπολογιστή τους και κάποιοι δεν κατάλαβαν τι εννοούσε. Ήταν άνετοι χρησιμοποιώντας υπολογιστές, αλλά η οργάνωση αρχείων σε φακέλους και καταλόγους ήταν άγνωστη σε ορισμένους. Η εμπειρία του Garland παρουσιάστηκε σε ένα άρθρο του 2021 The Verge σχετικά με ένα εκπληκτικό κενό στους νέους…
items.descriptionOriginal: Engineering professor Catherine Garland asked her students where they’d saved their computer files , and some didn’t understand what she meant. They were comfortable using computers , but organizing files into folders and directories was unfamiliar to some. Garland’s experience was featured in a 2021 The Verge article about a surprising gap in young people’s computer skills. Although many students have grown up using smartphones, tablets, and laptops, that doesn’t necessarily mean they understand how files are stored and organized. Working on a laptop at school. Photo Credit: Canva Why do some students struggle to find their files? The problem first caught Garland’s attention in 2017 while she was teaching an engineering course. Students were using software to simulate jet-engine turbines. Some encountered error messages because the program couldn’t locate their files. Garland tried to help by asking where they’d saved their work. Had they put it on the desktop? Was it on a shared drive? Some students didn’t understand the questions. As Garland explained in The Verge article, “They see it like one bucket, and everything’s in the bucket.” Other instructors described similar experiences. Lincoln Colling, a psychology lecturer at the University of Sussex, recalled asking students to retrieve a file from a specific directory, only to be met with blank stares. Nicolás Guarín-Zapata , an applied physicist and lecturer at Universidad EAFIT in Colombia, also noticed students struggling to find their documents. He began teaching basic computer organization at the start of each semester, including how files and folders work. Older computer interfaces often required users to navigate through folders to locate their work. Today, search functions and apps can make that process largely unnecessary. Someone can open a document without ever thinking about which folder contains it. That convenience can become a problem when students encounter software that requires them to know exactly where a file is stored. Young students in an innovative robotics class. Photo Credit: Canva Growing up with technology doesn’t mean knowing everything about it A 2026 study published in the Journal of Statistics and Data Science Education examined computer literacy among university students taking introductory statistical programming courses in Germany. Researchers found considerable differences in students’ computer experience and confidence with everyday tasks. Most students felt comfortable creating documents, downloading files, and using search engines. But confidence was less consistent for tasks such as managing files, installing programs, and using operating-system search functions. Although nearly all students used smartphones daily, their experience with desktop computers varied considerably. The findings suggest that regularly using digital devices doesn’t necessarily make students confident with every computer task. A teacher helping students on the computer. Photo Credit: Canva Teaching the skills students haven’t learned Agnes Cameron , a specialist technician at the University of the Arts London’s Creative Computing Institute, developed workshops to help students build basic computer skills. According to her January 2026 teaching case study , the workshops included practical activities involving image editing and web design. They were designed to help students become more comfortable using computers and the software required for their coursework. A “New skills” button on a computer keyboard. Photo Credit: Canva A simple computer skill that can make life easier Fortunately, the basics of file organization are fairly simple. A file is a document or piece of information saved on a computer. A folder holds files and can contain other folders. A file path identifies the location of a particular file within that structure. For example, a student saves an assignment inside a folder named “Schoolwork,” which sits inside their “Documents folder.” Knowing that location makes it easier to find the assignment later, especially if the application asks them to select a particular file. Garland eventually began rethinking her own approach to organizing files. She started using her computer’s search function to find schedules and documents instead of navigating through folders. “I’m like, huh … I don’t even need these subfolders,” Garland said. The post A professor asked students where they saved their work. Some didn’t understand the question. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Τα παιδιά έφτιαξαν ψηλότερους πύργους για σπαγγέτι από τους απόφοιτους σχολών επιχειρήσεων κάνοντας κάτι που οι ενήλικες ξέχασαν πώς να κάνουν
items.titleOriginal: Kids built taller spaghetti towers than business school grads by doing something adults forgot how to do
items.description: Ο Tom Wujec έχει περάσει χρόνια ταξιδεύοντας σε όλο τον κόσμο με μια χούφτα ξυλάκια σπαγγέτι. Ως μέρος των εταιρικών του εργαστηρίων για τη δημιουργία ομάδας, συχνά ζητά από τις ομάδες να κάνουν μια ανόητη, ανόητη εργασία: να φτιάξουν έναν πύργο από στεγνά μακαρόνια και ταινία, να τον κάνουν όσο το δυνατόν πιο ψηλό και να τον χτίσουν αρκετά δυνατό ώστε να κρατήσει το βάρος ενός marshmallow. Α, και κάντε το γρήγορα.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Tom Wujec has spent years traveling the globe with a handful of spaghetti sticks. As part of his corporate team-building workshops, he often asks groups to do a silly, counterintuitive task: build a tower out of dry spaghetti and tape, make it as tall as possible, and build it strong enough to hold the weight of one marshmallow. Oh, and do it fast. “The Marshmallow Challenge is a fun and instructive design exercise that encourages teams to work in these conditions to learn profound lessons in collaboration, innovation, and creativity,” he says. “It’s simple, fun, and instructive.” But now, having done the exercise with groups of all ages and backgrounds around the world, he’s learned a lot about who succeeds at the challenge and who struggles. Kids routinely outperform business school grads in marshmallow challenge A surprising group repeatedly appears in Wujec’s data and observations as having difficulty with the Marshmallow Challenge : “On every measure… the group that consistently does the worst is recent graduates of business school. MBA students. They suck. They’re terrible,” he teases in a TED Talk. As for groups that do well? The usual suspects, of course: engineers and architects. But another group seems to shine wherever Wujec takes his bundle of supplies: kindergarteners and all manner of young school kids. Why kids are amazing at building fast Wujec says that many of the groups he studies, and especially the business students, waste a lot of time. They have 18 minutes to complete their tower, and many adults spend a good portion of that time debating ideas and jockeying for leadership within the group. Then, they spend far too long planning and strategizing. You might expect kids to be exceedingly creative and good at thinking outside the box, and that’s true. Wujec notes that groups of kids come up with wild, truly unique designs that adults can’t conceive. But the other thing kids do well is fail. They’re not afraid of their tower falling down. So what do they do? They build fast, running with the first good idea they come up with. If it doesn’t work, and the tower won’t hold the marshmallow? They simply start again, with plenty of time left on the clock to iterate or start over completely. “They start with the marshmallow. They generally don’t talk, they stick things in the marshmallow. The marshmallow falls over, and they fix it, and start over,” Wujec explains. So while the business school grads are deciding who’s the leader of the group and sketching out their vision, the kids are already on their third prototype. Kindergarteners don’t just outperform business school grads—they do better than the average of all the groups Wujec has tested, and regularly outperform some whip-smart folks like lawyers and CEOs. In a LinkedIn post, behavioral scientist Michael Rucker writes that adults often fear failure much more than children. When trying something new, kids can be scared for many reasons, but their approach not working is usually not one of them. They lead with curiosity and fun, and they see what happens. The Marshmallow Challenge is a wonderful reminder for adults: what would it look like to just go for it? No waiting for permission, no jockeying for authority, just grabbing the marshmallow and going to work, knowing that every time it falls down, you’re one step closer to the ultimate goal, whatever it may be. The post Kids built taller spaghetti towers than business school grads by doing something adults forgot how to do appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Έρευνα αποκαλύπτει 5 μεγάλους λόγους που οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι που δεν πίνουν κρατούν τη νηφαλιότητά τους μυστική από τους άλλους
items.titleOriginal: Survey reveals 5 big reasons most non-drinkers keep their sobriety a secret from others
items.description: Η ποπ κουλτούρα απεικονίζει την κατανάλωση αλκοόλ ως έναν πανταχού παρόν κανόνα στην αμερικανική ζωή. Σε ταινίες και τηλεοπτικές εκπομπές, φίλοι «πιάνουν μια μπύρα» μαζί, βγαίνουν ραντεβού για ποτά, οι καλεσμένοι φέρνουν κρασί ως δώρο και οι άνθρωποι γιορτάζουν κάθε μεγάλο γεγονός της ζωής με σαμπάνια. Αλλά ένας εκπληκτικός αριθμός Αμερικανών στην πραγματικότητα δεν πίνουν καθόλου. Σύμφωνα με την Gallup, μόνο το 54%…
items.descriptionOriginal: Pop culture portrays drinking alcohol as a ubiquitous norm in American life. In films and TV shows, friends “grab a beer” together, dates “meet up for drinks,” guests bring wine as a gift, and people celebrate any an every big life event with champagne. But a surprising number of Americans don’t actually drink at all. According to Gallup , only 54% of adults in the U.S. drink alcohol, even occasionally. That means close to half of Americans don’t drink at all. One reason that number may be surprising is that a lot of sober folks are tight-lipped about it. In fact, a Boca Recovery Center survey found that 58% of non-drinkers hide their sobriety from certain people in their lives and 13% keep it a secret from everyone. But why? Let’s dive into the reasons behind the data. "The share of Americans who say they drink alcohol remains at a record-low 54% for the second consecutive year, the lowest reading in Gallup’s trend dating back to 1939." (via @gallup ) https://t.co/wzmiLyl19l pic.twitter.com/z6DcUkzDLG — John Gramlich (@johngramlich) August 20, 2026 Why fewer people are drinking Gallup data shows that in 1978, 71% of Americans drank alcohol, the highest in the past eight decades. In 2026, drinking hit a record low of 54%. There are lots of reasons people choose sobriety. Some people don’t like the way alcohol makes them feel. Others stop drinking after developing an addiction to it. Some observe religious prohibitions on alcohol. Others don’t want the excess calories. Some might be taking a medication that is contraindicated with alcohol. Others just hate the taste. The health risks of alcohol have become a bigger consideration for many, according to Gallop. In 2016, only 26% of people believed that having one or two drinks per day was bad for your health. In 2026, nearly double that number—51%—say it’s unhealthy. And in the Boca Secret Sobriety Report, half of non-drinkers said they stopped drinking for their physical or mental health. Why do people hide their sobriety? Boca’s Secret Sober Report goes into the numbers of people who keep their sober status private from at least some people (58%), as well as the reasons people give for not revealing that they don’t drink. View this post on Instagram More than half keep it from their social media followers as well as from their manager or supervisor. More than a third keep it from people they’ve dated since quitting or from their coworkers. One in four don’t tell their friends and acquaintances they’re sober, and one in five don’t tell their family members. About 13% keep it secret from everyone. The most common reason for not telling people, which 65% of respondents indicated, is “It didn’t seem like a big deal.” After that, 19% said, “It’s too personal,” 15% wanted to avoid questions, 13% didn’t want to be labeled, and 13% didn’t want to be judged. How the numbers break down by generation Of the 13% of people who don’t tell anyone they’re sober, here’s the generational split: Gen X: 20% Millennials: 12% Baby boomers: 10% Gen Z: 5% Of the 50% of respondents who don’t drink for their mental or physical health: Gen X: 54% Millennials: 52% Baby boomers: 45% Gen Z: 44% Of the 25% of Americans who have tried an alcohol-free challenges, such as a 30-Day Break or Dry January: Millennials: 29% Gen Z: 26% Gen X: 23% Baby boomers: 10% Overall, even though they drink less than younger generations previously have, Gen Z still feels more pressure to drink than other generations do. In the Boca report, 69% of sober Gen Zers said they’ve been questioned, pressured, or teased about not drinking, compared to 49% of other sober Americans. Tips for navigating the social drinking vs. sobriety landscape There appears to be a glaring contradiction in some of the data, which may boil down to perception. The vast majority of respondents—a whopping 94%—said that a person doesn’t owe anyone an explanation for why they’re not drinking. Additionally, 93% of people said they wouldn’t think less of a coworker who doesn’t drink at an event. However, 52% of sober Americans say they’ve been questioned, pressured, or teased about not drinking. And 30% said they’ve disguised not drinking to blend in, such as giving a fake reason for not drinking or ordering a drink they didn’t intend to consume. So most people express that they’re okay with people not drinking, but that’s not always how it feels on the sober side of things. Boca offers these tips for protecting your sobriety when you know you’re going to be at an event where people are drinking: Keep a short answer ready: A simple, honest line like “I’m not drinking tonight” is usually enough, and it saves you from inventing a reason on the spot. Choose your own drink early: Ordering a soda, mocktail, or sparkling water as soon as you arrive can head off offers before they start. Tell one trusted person: Sharing your decision with a friend or coworker you trust gives you an ally who can help redirect the conversation. Give yourself permission to leave: If an event starts to feel like too much pressure, it’s okay to step outside or head home early. And for those who do drink and don’t want sober folks to feel pressured or judged: Avoid teasing people about not drinking (even good-natured teasing can be uncomfortable), offer non-alcoholic options as a legitimate choice and not a lesser alternative, and don’t dwell on the person’s choice not to drink. Treat it as the no big deal that it is. No one should feel like they need to hide being sober to fit in or avoid scrutiny. We can all let each other have our individual choices and preferences without judging anyone either direction. You can find the full Secret Sober Report from Boca Recovery Center here. The post Survey reveals 5 big reasons most non-drinkers keep their sobriety a secret from others appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ένα τεστ καρδιάς σε δύο λεπτά: Πώς οι ιδρυτές του Dehradun κατασκεύασαν μια συσκευή ΗΚΓ σε μέγεθος τσέπης
items.titleOriginal: A Heart Test in Two Minutes: How Dehradun Founders Built a Pocket-Sized ECG Device
items.description: Για κάποιον που βιώνει πόνο στο στήθος ή δύσπνοια σε ένα απομακρυσμένο χωριό, η λήψη ΗΚΓ μπορεί να σημαίνει ότι θα ταξιδέψει αρκετά χιλιόμετρα στο πλησιέστερο νοσοκομείο. Μέχρι να γίνει η δοκιμή, πολύτιμα λεπτά μπορεί να έχουν ήδη χαθεί. Αυτό το κενό ήταν που οδήγησε τον Rajat Jain και τους συνιδρυτές του να δημιουργήσουν τη Sunfox Technologies, μια εταιρεία τεχνολογίας υγείας στο Dehradun,…
items.descriptionOriginal: For someone experiencing chest pain or breathlessness in a remote village, getting an ECG can mean travelling several kilometres to the nearest hospital. By the time the test is done, precious minutes may already have been lost. It was this gap that led Rajat Jain and his co-founders to build Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech company in Dehradun, Uttarakhand. They launched Spandan, a pocket-sized ECG device that connects to a smartphone. The device can record a medical-grade ECG and generate a report within minutes, without needing a conventional ECG machine, an external battery or an internet connection. Today, more than 60,000 Spandan devices have been deployed across India, reaching over 20,000 villages across 28 states. The technology has been used to screen around five million patients, and over 2,00,000 lives have been saved. The journey to making cardiac testing more accessible, however, began with a personal tragedy that changed the course of Rajat's life. The personal loss that started it For Rajat, the idea for Sunfox began with a loss that was difficult to make sense of. At 21, he lost a close friend to a heart attack. The experience made him realise that cardiac emergencies can strike without warning and that, even when help is available, the first few minutes can make a crucial difference. At the time, Rajat was a mechanical engineer working in the automotive field. But the loss made him look towards a problem that felt far more urgent: "How could technology make basic cardiac diagnosis available when a hospital or specialist was not close by?" Bill Gates listening to Rajat Jain demonstrate Spandan's prowess at ICMR HQ in Delhi. Spandan was selected among India's best healthcare innovations supported by ICMR. That question led him and his co-founders — Arpit Jain, Saurabh Badola, Nitin Chandola and Sabit Rawat — to start Sunfox Technologies in Dehradun in 2016. They began working on ways to make an ECG, one of the first tests doctors use when a patient shows signs of a heart problem, smaller, more affordable and easier to use. The prototype was developed in 2017, laying the groundwork for the company's effort to take cardiac screening into places where access to specialised care is limited. How a smartphone became an ECG machine An ECG, or electrocardiogram, records the tiny electrical signals the heart produces with every beat. Doctors use it to identify a heart attack, a blocked artery or an irregular heartbeat. Traditionally, it requires a large machine, a trained technician and a hospital room. Spandan changes that. It is a portable 12-lead ECG device that connects to a smartphone, records the heart's signals and produces a report in about two minutes. "The advantage of using Spandan is that anyone with or without medical education can use it," says Jain. "Spandan devices use ECG sensors, smartphone integration, and software to record and display ECGs. It uses AI and analytics for report generation," he explains. "Also, it does not need an external battery to work; it uses power from your smartphone to work." That design was a deliberate choice, made with rural India in mind. "These features were very important for us as the device had to work in remote locations in the country without a regular source of electricity or internet connection," says Rajat. While the devices range in price from Rs 6,900 to Rs 75,000, depending on the model, Sunfox says a significant share of its users come from smaller towns and rural areas. Around 60 per cent of its users are from rural or semi-urban locations, with more than 20,000 devices currently active in these regions. Co-founders of Sunfox Technologies. Small clinics are among the buyers, as they see value in the device even at the Rs 16,000–17,000 price point, says the company. For healthcare facilities with limited access to conventional ECG machines, a portable device that can generate reports within minutes offers another way to conduct cardiac screening. For Sunfox, the goal was to make a heart test as routine as other everyday health checks, without hurting the wallet. Making cardiac monitoring accessible at home The device is also being used by individuals who want to monitor their heart health between doctor visits. Sandip Deodhar, 52, an accountant assistant from Kolhapur, has been using Spandan for the past month. He is hypertensive and diabetic, and says he would often spend Rs 200–300 every other week on ECG tests recommended during his consultations. After discovering Spandan online, he discussed it with his doctor, who agreed that he could use the device to record ECGs at home. "For the first three-four days, I ran multiple tests to review the reports and become accustomed to the device. Now, he tells me to notify him only if there is an abnormal test; otherwise, he says there's no need to even show him the report," says Sandip. The pilot: Testing in a hospital Before Spandan could go to villages, it had to prove itself inside a hospital. "We did the pilot in Fortis Hospital in Uttarakhand in 2018-19 along with SELCO Foundation," shares Rajat. The team wanted answers to two questions. "We were trying to prove the validity and accuracy of our devices and wanted to know how user-friendly our devices are so that frontline health workers with minimal trainin g could operate them." Then, in 2021, a study was conducted at Fortis Escorts Hospital in Dehradun under the supervision of cardiologists. The patients were first tested on the hospital's standard ECG machine. Within five minutes, the same patients were tested on Spandan, and a cardiologist reviewed the readings independently. Of the 153 patients enrolled, 110 were counted in the final results, and Spandan's reading matched that of the standard machine in 108 of those 110 cases. It was a small study, but it provided a base for what followed. Larger hospital studies came next, including a study of 2,799 patients, published in 2025 in the Anatolian Journal of Cardiology , and one in Meerut involving 184 patients with chest pain. The company says the count is now 30 studies. "We have compared the performance of Spandan with standard ECG devices in more than 30,000 patients and have achieved a 99.7% accuracy," says Rajat. How Sunfox found its footing Proving Spandan in a hospital was one step. Getting it into the field brought a different set of challenges. The first problem was money. "The biggest challenge for us was overcoming a funding crunch while developing a health device, which conventionally requires a large investment," says Rajat. In the early days, the founders paid for the work themselves. "When we first started, there was no funding or grant. We self-sponsored in most part and also did side-gigs to support the research and development of our devices," he recalls. The second problem was testing the device where it was meant to be used. A hospital in Dehradun is very different from a village clinic, and a device built for villages had to be tried in villages. "Secondly, we had difficulty in validating the results of our device in low-resource and rural areas because we couldn't get too many patients there," says Jain. There was also the matter of trust. Sunfox was entering India's medical device sector, which is known for high entry barriers, strict rules, heavy investment and a market crowded with imported products. Rajat says, "We faced constant doubts about whether medical technology built in India could be trusted." Help arrived in stages. In 2017, the first prototype was ready, and the team moved into its first office at a technology incubator at Graphic Era University in Dehradun. Government funding followed. "Later, we received funding from the state government of Uttarakhand, from our university, and also from the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, to conduct the pilot tests," says Jain. Private money came next. "In 2022, Sunfox appeared on Shark Tank India, where we got funding of Rs 1 crore," adds Rajat. Larger funding has followed since. In August 2024, Sunfox raised Rs 15 crore in a round led by Venture Catalysts. Inc42 also reports that the company had earlier received Rs 5 crore from USAID through its SAMRIDH Health programme and LetsVenture. Now the product had to be tested in real-life settings. Government partnerships gave Sunfox access to rural clinics. In September 2026, Sunfox raised $7 million (INR 66 crore) in a Series A funding round led by renowned investor Ashish Kacholia, Lashit Sanghvi, Alchemy Capital and 3one4 Capital. The real-life challenge Now the product had to be tested in real-life settings. Government partnerships gave Sunfox access to rural clinics. In December 2020, the Government of India's biotech agency BIRAC and the industry body Nasscom launched JanCare, a challenge offering health-tech startups pilot test beds at rural health centres in partnership with state governments. Sunfox took part, deploying eight devices across six CHCs and PHCs in Nagaland and two CHCs in Uttar Pradesh. In July 2022, Sunfox also worked with the Uttarakhand government to set up a free screening camp at Sonprayag, where the Kedarnath trek begins. Trained local volunteers screened pilgrims with Spandan and sent abnormal readings over WhatsApp to a cardiologist in Dehradun. In the first month, the camp screened nearly 1,500 people and referred 59 to a local doctor. These pilots showed that health workers without specialist training could operate the device, and larger deployments followed. SAMRIDH, the USAID-backed programme, says its support helped place 1,551 Spandan units in public and private clinics across Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Delhi, screening 63,486 people. From a prototype to 60,000 devices What began as a self-funded lab in Dehradun has since grown into a nationwide deployment. More than 60,000 Spandan devices are now in use, covering over 20,000 villages. "We have deployed over 60,000 devices in the country, from Himalayan states like Uttarakhand to Nagaland in the North-east and heavily forested and remote areas in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand," says Rajat. State governments have come on board. "We are working with the state governments of Uttarakhand and Haryana so that any patient with symptoms of heart ailments can get access to quick diagnosis and treatment," he says. The two-minute turnaround is particularly significant in these settings. "The healthcare worker, whether a nurse, technician or even doctor, puts the leads on the patient and receives an ECG within 3 minutes, with a clinician-reviewed diagnosis and prescription," Jain explains. The results show up in the numbers. Until October 2026, "In Uttarakhand, we have worked in CHCs and PHCs on the Char Dham Yatra route and have screened more than 13100 pilgrims and identified 463 critical patients who could receive treatment on time," he says. In Haryana, "We have deployed our devices in more than 597 PHCs and CHCs and conducted ECGs for 60,000 people and detected 2000 critical cases since June." The device can also flag the most dangerous kind of heart attack early. "We can detect the deadliest kind of heart attack, called STEMI, in less than an hour of it first occurring, saving thousands of lives," says Jain. The road ahead In August 2026, Sunfox marked 10 years with the opening of an innovation hub in Dehradun. Its next goal is to take Spandan beyond India. "We plan to expand in low- and middle-income countries, especially in Africa and South Asia, and we have already started." According to SAMRIDH, more than 400 Spandan devices are in use across Africa. The mission has not changed since the day Jain lost his friend. "Most heart attacks in India are preventable if diagnosed early," he says. "Our vision is to take this portable ECG technology and make it so ubiquitous that everyone has access to it, just as they do for thermometers and BP machines." And if the numbers are anything to go by, Sunfox is surely on its way to success.

items.title: Ο Billy Corgan σοκάρει το αστέρι του «Breakfast Club» εξηγώντας γιατί η ταινία αποτυπώνει τέλεια τον πόνο Gen X
items.titleOriginal: Billy Corgan shocks ‘Breakfast Club’ star by explaining why the film perfectly captures Gen X pain
items.description: Σε ένα πρόσφατο επεισόδιο του podcast The Magnificent Others, ο οικοδεσπότης της σειράς και frontman των Smashing Pumpkins, Billy Corgan, προσπάθησε να μοιραστεί μια νέα άποψη για το The Breakfast Club που ο καλεσμένος του, ο ηθοποιός Anthony Michael Hall, δεν είχε ξανακούσει. Ο Hall παραδέχτηκε ότι δεν μπορεί να μείνει μια μέρα χωρίς να μιλήσει για το κλασικό Gen X, οπότε ο Corgan έκοψε τη δουλειά του…
items.descriptionOriginal: On a recent episode of The Magnificent Others podcast, the show’s host and Smashing Pumpkins frontman, Billy Corgan, attempted to share a fresh perspective on The Breakfast Club that his guest, actor Anthony Michael Hall, had never heard before. Hall admitted he can’t go a day without talking about the Gen X classic , so Corgan had his work cut out for him. In the 1985 John Hughes classic, Hall played Brian Johnson, known as “The Brain.” “A lot of us were the latchkey kids. And the joke I always make is we were abandoned by our parents because of [deleted] and yoga,” Corgan joked. “So the reason I think that movie resonated so deeply? It’s kind of this bullying thing. I see that as a subplot. I think the key is all these kids have been abandoned by the people they should be relying on.” Why is ‘The Breakfast Club’ so important to Gen Xers? “I go to the most obvious point, the dynamics between the characters, let’s call it the kineticism between the characters. But the thing that started to strike me was, wait, they’re all in detention for a reason. And so, the subtext in my mind is they’ve been abandoned by something or somebody,” Corgan continued. Corgan taps into the idea that Gen Xers (1965 to 1980) are often called the least parented generation because they grew up when divorce was at an all-time high, more women were in the workplace , and children were allowed to roam free. In some ways, Gen Xers had incredible freedom that today’s kids should envy. In other ways, growing up as a latchkey kid or with parents who weren’t around was tantamount to neglect. Hall agreed with Corgans’ take. “You’re right. The loss that they all feel may be from their parents and what they’re not doing,” he responded. In the film, Allison Reynolds, the “Basket Case,” is clearly neglected by her parents. She tells Emilio Estevez’s character, “They ignore me.” Her strange behavior throughout the film feels like an attempt to be seen. The characters in ‘The Breakfast Club’ are all dealing with some form of neglect “When I think back on the film, I think it’s most clearly seen in Ally Sheedy’s character [“The Basket Case”]. That sense of neglect from her parents,” Hall added. “So, that’s a key word, and you brought up something really powerful here, which is what the parents weren’t doing that led them there.” The rest of the main characters in The Breakfast Club weren’t necessarily neglected in the sense that they weren’t given any attention, but they all lack a real emotional connection to their parents, which is just as painful. John “The Criminal” Bender is verbally and physically abused by his father, leading him to be rebellious. Claire “The Princess” Standish is used as a weapon in her parents’ marriage woes, making her feel like a pawn. Andrew “The Athlete” Clark’s parents push him too hard to win and be tough; he becomes a bully to overcompensate. Brian “The Brain” Johnson, Hall’s character, is so concerned with his grades that a bad mark makes him consider self-harm. In the end, the five teenagers from different social classes and cliques learn to lean on each other to get through detention and tell the principal that they are beyond categorization. Corgan believes this type of camaraderie mirrors the attitudes of kids in the alternative rock scene of the ’80s and ’90s that gave birth to the Smashing Pumpkins. “But at the end of the day, the reason I think it hits so hard is almost everybody in our generation was thinking ‘that’s me’ in that same dynamic, having to reach for people,” Corgan said. “One of the core ethos of alternative rock was we found community with a bunch of other weirdos because many of us were the land of lost toys. Who were we going to turn to?” The post Billy Corgan shocks ‘Breakfast Club’ star by explaining why the film perfectly captures Gen X pain appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Spacecraft could soon share a common refueling connection, potentially changing how operators manage satellites in orbit. Spaceium has released OpenPort, an open-source interface that any company can license and manufacture for just $1. The design lets spacecraft receive fuel after launch instead of relying entirely on their onboard reserves. It will also undergo an orbital demonstration aboard the International Space Station. Common refueling standard Most satellites carry a fixed supply of propellant for their planned missions. Once that supply runs low, operators often retire otherwise functional spacecraft. Their electronics and other systems might remain operational, but limited fuel can end their usefulness. A lack of standardized connections has also complicated orbital refueling efforts. Different manufacturers develop their own interfaces, forcing operators to consider compatibility before arranging fuel transfers. A tanker built by one company might not connect with another manufacturer’s spacecraft. OpenPort aims to address that problem through an identical connection on both spacecraft. Its androgynous design allows either vehicle to supply or receive propellant. That means a satellite could potentially refuel another spacecraft instead of relying exclusively on dedicated tankers. The interface also replaces a conventional fill-and-drain valve. Those connections typically serve ground fueling operations before launch. OpenPort keeps the connection functional after a spacecraft reaches orbit. Spaceium says its design handles higher pressures and greater docking misalignment than competing refueling interfaces. These capabilities could help spacecraft establish reliable connections during demanding orbital operations. Xenon transfer reaches orbit OpenPort’s upcoming demonstration will take place aboard the International Space Station. Spaceium plans to fly the hardware as a NASA-approved external payload through Voyager Technologies’ commercial payload service. During the demonstration, the interface will transfer xenon between two tanks in orbit. Spaceium describes this as the first-ever xenon transfer performed in orbit. The mission will test whether spacecraft can exchange propellant through a standardized connection. The demonstration follows another Spaceium mission in February 2026. Its precision robotic actuator successfully completed its first space mission after launching aboard a SpaceX rideshare. Building a refueling network Spaceium wants OpenPort to become a widely adopted connection across the spacecraft industry. Its broader business model centers on automated orbital stations that sell propellant as a service. Co-founder and CEO Ashi Dissanayake says the company sees the stations as its primary business. Every spacecraft equipped with OpenPort could eventually become a potential customer. “The port isn’t the business. The stations are,” Dissanayake said . He believes widespread adoption will create demand for orbital refueling services, including those operated by competitors. Founded by aerospace and mechanical engineers Dissanayake and Reza Fetanat, Spaceium joined Y Combinator’s Summer 2024 batch. Its commercial customers include operators pursuing orbital transfer vehicles, lunar missions and geostationary satellites. The company plans to establish refueling stations across low Earth orbit and geostationary orbit. Its longer-term ambitions also include stations along routes to the Moon. A common connection could eventually help satellite operators extend spacecraft lifespans. It could also allow lunar missions and orbital transfer vehicles to travel farther without carrying all their propellant from Earth. Spaceium is expanding its engineering team as it prepares for the ISS demonstration and its first refueling station. OpenPort’s adoption will ultimately determine whether different spacecraft manufacturers embrace a shared standard.

items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems , a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway. Why microplastics are hard to remove Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it. “We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.” Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue , and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure. How the technology works PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu , trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy. The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue. Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.” “I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.” Where PolyGone goes from here A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve noticed more spiders lately, near window frames, behind boxes in the garage, lurking in basement corners, you’re not imagining it. Fall is mating season for spiders , which makes them more active than usual, and when temperatures drop, many of them make the same call you would and head inside. Of the roughly 3,700 spider species in the United States, only about 0.3 percent are dangerous to humans. The rest are, in the words of Oregon State University Extension horticulturist Brooke Edmunds , “minding their own business.” Two things converging in the spiderverse It’s not only the cold driving these arachnids indoors. Spiders like cellar spiders, wolf spiders, and hobo spiders move indoors as temperatures fall, and once inside, many are also looking for mates and somewhere quiet to leave their eggs . “Just like us, they’re coming inside to get warm,” Edmunds explains. “They aren’t aggressive toward people, not even the spiders.” Some females carry egg sacs on their bodies; others are hunting for corners, furniture undersides, the back of a closet, anywhere spider silk can hold a sac in place. That’s part of why fall can feel like a sudden invasion when it’s really just two instincts running in parallel. What makes your home The Destination Some of it is biology, and some of it is a gap in the garage door seal. If the weather strip at the bottom is worn or the door doesn’t sit flush, that’s an open invitation. Same goes for cracks along the foundation and gaps around window frames. And if your house already has gnats, flies, aphids, or termites, spiders will follow, because those critters happen to make up a great menu for our eight-legged friends. Outside, what’s close to the house does a lot of the inviting. Colorado State University’s entomology experts recommend clearing away rock piles, wood stacks, old boards, and compost heaps from around the perimeter. Spiders go for dark, damp, undisturbed spots. Tree limbs that touch or hang near windows are another way in, and crawl spaces packed with boxes are definitely attractive to them. How to keep them out Caulking cracks in your foundation and making sure screens and door seals are intact does a lot. Fall is also a good time to go through basements, garages, and closets, not for tidiness, but because those neglected corners are exactly what spiders are looking for. If you’re digging into old cardboard boxes or boots that haven’t moved since last winter, wear gloves. Spiders have sometimes made a cozy home inside them. If you’d rather not evict the ones already there, that’s fine too. They’re eating the insects you’d otherwise be swatting at, and most will move on once the season turns anyway. items.descriptionOriginal: We like to think we always know the right thing to do. Some lessons, however, come the hard way . We learn through mistakes and missteps, stumbling into victories through trial and error. Some lessons, it seems, we have to learn on our own, no matter what other people have tried to tell us. There are also hard truths that come from quiet reflection or mulling over guidance passed down from a mentor . Now add random internet comment sections to that list. A popular Reddit thread recently asked users to share the one piece of advice that permanently altered their perspective. The responses offer a powerful reminder to listen closely to others’ wisdom. Here are 10 life-changing pieces of advice that might just reshape your own journey. 1. Ask which choice lets you be who you really are. “When I consider options, I ask which choice lets me become more of myself? It doesn’t mean ‘always choose whatever feels good.’ Sometimes becoming more yourself requires doing something difficult, disciplined, or terrifying.” We often make decisions based on comfort or fear. This may seem like the easier route, but is it more beneficial for you in the long run? Asking which path brings you closer to your true self shifts the focus completely. Growth rarely happens inside our comfort zones. 2. Never pass up an opportunity to use the restroom. ” It has NEVER failed me to be proactive.” Anyone who has ever been stuck in gridlock traffic knows the profound truth of this rule. Urgency doesn’t always lead to the best options. Proactive comfort is an underrated life hack. 3. Be forgiving; it sure helps. A quote often misattributed to various speakers (Buddha, Saint Augustine, Nelson Mandela, etc.) goes: “Holding a grudge is like drinking poison and waiting for the other person to die.” Whoever said it, the message is clear: forgiveness is as much for you as it is for the other person. No one is saying you have to forget, either. This is about freeing yourself from another person’s emotional baggage. 4. Accentuate the positive. “If you’ve spent years conditioning yourself to think negatively about yourself, you can condition yourself in the other direction too. It might feel cheesy at first but keep reinforcing the positive until that starts becoming your default mindset. Just embrace the cheesiness for now and do it anyway.” Neural pathways take time to rewire. Your brain believes what you tell it every day. Embracing a little cheesiness is a small price to pay to push yourself toward a more positive path. 5. Stop expecting everyone else to act like you. “Not everyone thinks like I do – and that’s ok.” This one hits deep. We often get hurt when people don’t react, work, or care the way we do. The spark of your passion does not have to be lit by others. Realizing that everyone operates from their own blueprint can save you lots of heartbreak. 6. It’s an expense, not a problem. “A problem that can be solved with money isn’t a problem; it’s an expense.” Perspective changes everything when life throws a curveball. A flat tire or a broken appliance can feel devastating in the moment, so don’t add fuel to the fire. Remembering that it is a financial hurdle, not a life-or-death situation, helps keep stress in check. 7. Nobody will thank you for living up to their expectations. “Stop people-pleasing.” No one wants to be someone else’s source of stress, but people-pleasing is a quiet trap. At the end of the day, you are the one who has to live with your choices. Live a life that makes sense to you. 8. How much time did you spend thinking about other people’s mistakes today? “It wasn’t much, right? I stopped caring so much about what others think of me at that moment. I started making more decisions without regrets.” We spend so much energy worrying about how others judge us. In reality, most people are too focused on themselves to worry about you most of the time. Recognizing this truth brings instant freedom. 9. Say no to some things so you can say yes to others. “Totally changed my POV. That was thirty years ago, and it has informed my successful career.” Understanding your limits is important, especially in business. Every single “yes” you give away is a hidden “no” to your own time and priorities. Protecting your energy ensures you have enough left for what truly matters, both at work and at home. 10. Empathy with boundaries is compassion. Empathy without boundaries is self-destruction. “Needed to hear this right now. Thank you.” There are plenty of things in this world that spark concern and worry. Compassion is what connects us , building bridges of understanding and community. But you cannot pour from an empty cup. Caring deeply for others should never require you to sacrifice your own mental health or safety. Give, but give what you can afford. The post People share 10 ‘random pieces of advice’ that legitimately changed their lives appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Τα άτομα που φτάνουν νωρίς σε συναντήσεις, ραντεβού ή hangout έχουν σαφώς καλές δεξιότητες διαχείρισης χρόνου . Αλλά μπορεί να υπάρχει ένας βαθύτερος λόγος για την αμεσότητά τους: καλλιεργεί μια αίσθηση ηρεμίας. «Το να φτάσετε νωρίς είναι ένας τρόπος να δώσετε στο νευρικό σας σύστημα λίγο χρόνο να προσαρμοστεί και να εγκατασταθεί», λέει στο Upw η Chloë Bean, LMFT, θεραπεύτρια σωματικού τραύματος στο Λος Άντζελες.…
items.descriptionOriginal: People who arrive early to meetings, appointments, or hangouts clearly have good time-management skills . But there may be a deeper reason for their promptness : it fosters a sense of calm. “Arriving early is a way to give your nervous system some time to adjust and settle in,” Chloë Bean , LMFT, a somatic trauma therapist in Los Angeles, tells Upworthy. “If you have anxiety around transitions or being in unfamiliar spaces, it gives you time to orient to your surroundings.” Being early may seem rigid to some, but for those who always arrive early, it’s not simply about needing control. “There is a distinct quality of an ‘early person’ having that need to have a level of control to actually remain flexible,” explains Nicole Issa , Psy.D., founder and licensed psychologist at The Center for Dynamic and Behavioral Therapy. “These sound polar opposite. But that ability to prioritize being early means they can probably cope very well when things don’t go to plan.” Their duality is one of the many unique personality traits they possess. Personality traits of people who are always early Besides seeking a sense of calm, these are six personality traits and strengths that people who arrive early also have, according to psychologists and therapists: Personality trait No. 1: They strive for emotional self-regulation Rather than just simple time management, Issa tells Upworthy that people who arrive early may plan like this to avoid last-minute pressures that leave them feeling out of control or frustrated because they’re late. “You might refer to this type of person as conscientious,” she says. “They might already know how they’ll feel if they’re the last to arrive, and it could be the driver for anxiety or stress, so avoiding that at all costs could very well become a priority for them.” Personality trait No. 2: They are reliable Arriving early also correlates with being intentional, Bean tells Upworthy. “This person shows up when they say they’re going to. You can plan your evening around plans with them because they take the commitment very seriously,” she says. “This makes them the friend or co-worker you can rely on every single time.” Personality trait No. 3: They are methodical “People who arrive early may have a methodical approach to everyday life,” Savannah Matlock, LCSW, a licensed clinical social worker, tells Upworthy. “This means that they tend to think through the steps needed to accomplish something and plan accordingly. They also may consider potential obstacles (like what could cause them to be late) and take action to avoid them.” Personality trait No. 4: They’re adaptable People who prefer to arrive early are also good at anticipating possible outcomes and mentally preparing for them. “They might not appear flexible at first, but if things suddenly change, they usually have a plan in mind that will cover it, meaning emotionally they remain calm and able to move quickly and still achieve their goal of arriving early,” notes Issa. “For some of us, the sheer prospect of a curveball can mean a meltdown.” Personality trait No. 5: They are empathetic People who arrive early are usually thinking about how arriving late will impact others—and how it will affect how others view them. “So, being late can mean trust is ultimately broken, or they might feel, ‘I just can’t rely on this person anymore,'” explains Issa. “Coming from this perspective does require someone to have consideration for situations and others. It could be as simple as someone planning to arrive consistently early to make sure they don’t hurt someone’s feelings. Or, in the case of meetings, they avoid any kind of backlash.” Personality trait No. 6: They like to have options Bean adds that being early also gives people a sense of choice. “They might spot the best table by the window or see a dessert shop they want to check out after dinner,” she adds. The post Psychologists say people who are always early aren’t rigid, they have 6 distinct personality traits appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: On their podcast Beyond the Nest , hosts Allison and Lance Welch share stories and insights from their grandparenting journey—everything from managing an empty nest to deepening intimacy once parental obligations have dwindled. In an episode titled “The Roles of Healthy Grandparents & Their Effect on Kids,” the two talked about a familiar family phenomenon: grandparents who seem to have a much more lax approach to rules than parents do…or than they did when they were raising kids themselves. In other words, “spoiling.” Interestingly, Allison shared a social media story that put a slightly sweeter spin on this common complaint. A second chance for softness In the post, a mother recalled confronting her own mom after she let her grandchildren watch cartoons on her phone, even though the kids weren’t allowed to do that at home. The woman asked, “ Why can’t you say no to your grandkids when you said it to me a million times growing up? ” Her mother had an answer that made her see the situation a little differently. She explained that becoming a grandmother gave her a chance to experience motherhood again, but with a little more perspective. “I’m experiencing the little version of you all over again, but this time with more patience and a gentle kind of love.” “ And then it hit me, ” the woman wrote. “The extra snacks, the screen time, the bending of rules, not breaking…it isn’t her going against me, but it’s her loving my kids so much that sometimes those boundaries blur. And maybe that’s the beauty of being a grandmother. That she gets to love without limits the way she wished she could the first time with me.” “This time, I get to love the little version of you with more patience and a gentler kind of love.” A grandmother’s response when her daughter asked why she lets the grandkids break all the rules she was never allowed as a kid. The extra snacks, screen time, and bending… pic.twitter.com/PDfCCcyXOT — Camus (@newstart_2024) May 30, 2026 That idea seemed to resonate with a lot of people A short clip of the podcast was shared on X, and grandparents and adult children in the comments shared similar thoughts on why the grandparent-grandchild relationship can feel so different from the parent-child relationship. One person wrote, “My father gave my daughter the time he hadn’t had for me. It was his redemption, and we both knew it. It healed our relationship better than any words.” Another commenter summed up the difference this way: “More simply, a parent must prepare the child for life. That requires sternness. A grandparent’s job is to show love and joy. The parents have the hard job.” Meanwhile, on TikTok , one grandparent shared, “Being a grandpa changed how I felt about rules…the job is to give memories before you’re gone.” Of course, there is a difference between a grandparent giving a child an extra treat and one who routinely ignores the parents’ boundaries. The former can be part of the joy of being a grandparent. The latter can create real tension for everyone involved. That distinction came through in the comments, too “I’m definitely a gentler grandparent than I was a parent. That said, I follow the rules set down by the parents. I spoil with extra undivided attention I couldn’t give as a working parent,” noted one viewer. View this post on Instagram In other words, when it comes to family dynamics, including grandparent relationships, there can be room for boundaries and for grace. This conversation certainly doesn’t settle the question of how grandparents should behave, and it probably doesn’t need to. Families will have their own rules, relationships, and boundaries. But the discussion does offer an interesting look at why the bond between grandparents and grandchildren can feel so different from the one between parents and children. It can also invite a bit more compassion during times of frustration. Watch the full Beyond the Nest episode below: The post A mom questioned why grandma ‘spoils’ her kids. The answer changed her perspective. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Sweet potatoes are a shining star of Thanksgiving . From sweet potato casserole to sweet potato pie , it’s versatile enough to serve as both a side and a dessert. Japanese food blogger Yuri Yamamoto has shared a recipe that calls for using Japanese sweet potatoes (called “ satsuma-imo “), ideal for a Thanksgiving feast. On X, she shared her easy recipe for “sweet simmered sweet potatoes,” which she called “a gentle treat.” With just five simple ingredients, they take less than 10 minutes to make. “It’s a classic recipe, but it’s super easy to make in the microwave, and it’s handy for snacks, desserts, and packed lunches,” she explained, before adding, “They have a flavor that’s unique to this time of year, so give them a try if you’d like .” 優しいおやつ、さつまいもの甘煮。定番レシピですが、レンジでめっちゃ簡単に作れておやつにもデザートにもお弁当にも重宝します。 フライパンにバターを溶かしてこんがり表面を焼いて食べたり、市販の絞るだけホイップとともにパンに挟むのも最高！！ この時期ならではの美味しさなので良かったら pic.twitter.com/spEO5IlyLZ — 山本ゆり（syunkon レンジは600W) (@syunkon0507) November 11, 2026 Japanese sweet potato simmer recipe Yamamoto offers several ways to prepare and enjoy her Japanese sweet potato dessert. “You can also melt butter in a frying pan, brown them on the outside, and eat them that way. Or sandwich them in bread with store-bought whipped cream that you just squeeze out—absolutely delicious!!” she wrote. Here’s how to make them: Ingredients 1 sweet potato 2 tablespoon sugar 1 tablespoon mirin 1/2 tablespoon soy sauce 150ml (about 2/3 cup) water Instructions Wash 1 sweet potato (200–250g) well. Cut it into 1-centimeter-thick rounds, and soak in water for about 5 minutes. In a microwave-safe container (a bowl works too), mix 2 tablespoons sugar, 1 tablespoon mirin, 1/2 tbsp soy sauce, and 150ml (about 2/3 cup) water. Loosely cover and microwave for 4 minutes. Flip over and microwave for 2 minutes (add 1–2 minutes if still firm). Let cool so the flavors soak in. If you like, you can add salted butter or margarine while it’s hot, or sprinkle on black sesame seeds—both are great! Refrigerate for 3–4 days. Adjust the sweetness to taste—more or less is fine. *You can also make this in a pot. (Use 200 ml of water, just enough to barely cover the sweet potatoes. Cover and simmer for about 6 minutes.) ①さつまいも1本(200〜250g)はよく洗い1cm厚さの輪切りにし5分程水にさらす ②耐熱容器(ボウルでも)に［砂糖大2、みりん大1(なければ砂糖を少し増やす)、醤油小1/2、水150ml］を混ぜ①を入れ、フワッとラップor蓋をずらしてのせ4分チン ③裏返して2分チン(固ければ追加1〜2分)。冷まして染み込ませる pic.twitter.com/sCktheLQkl — 山本ゆり（syunkon レンジは600W) (@syunkon0507) November 11, 2026 What are Japanese sweet potatoes? Although sweet potatoes are not native to Japan, they arrived in the island country from Central America sometime in the 1600s, according to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs . They experienced a cultivation boom in 1732 after the shogun (military commander-in-chief and leader of the country) encouraged the Japanese people to grow them to prevent future food shortages and famine. Japanese sweet potatoes typically have reddish-purple skin and yellow flesh. However, over 60 varieties of Japanese sweet potatoes exist today. In 2019, Bon Appétit food writer Sarah Jampel described one popular Japanese sweet potato variety, the Murasaki (which is seasonably available at Trader Joe’s ), as this: “They’re simultaneously drier and creamier than orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, which means that when you roast them at high heat (cubes, wedges, circles, or halves, simply coated with olive oil and salt and cooked between 425 and 450°), their edges get unbelievably crispy and burnished, belying the pudding-like centers.” However you prepare them, they will make a great addition to your holiday table. The post A Japanese home cook shared a deliciously simple ‘sweet potato simmer’ dessert recipe that has Americans drooling appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Huddy Droubay had been waiting his turn. The 5-year-old from Syracuse, Utah, who has Down syndrome , watched his older brothers play soccer , and a little over a year ago, he finally joined a city league team himself. His mom, Melanie Droubay, posted a video of him out on the field. “The video got a couple million views because it was just him smiling the whole time,” she told KSL . “I don’t even know if he kicked the ball; he was just so happy to be on the field.” Serendipitously, one view came from superstar David Beckham. He commented that it was the sweetest smile he’d seen on a soccer pitch, or something close to it. “So, that was kind of the start of it all,” Droubay said. View this post on Instagram A few months later, Beckham sent Huddy a couple of signed jerseys with his name on them. Then, this past summer, a surprise package arrived with a letter from Beckham, now a co-owner of Inter Miami , inviting the whole family to a game. By then, Huddy had a name for him. His mother shared, “The ‘Mr. David’ part started when Huddy sang ‘Happy Birthday’ to David Beckham and sang ‘Happy birthday, Mr. David.’” On Wednesday, Oct. 28, before Inter Miami’s match against FC Cincinnati, the two finally met in the team’s locker room. In a video Droubay posted, Huddy hangs back for a moment before Beckham wins him over with a high-five and a hug. Beckham then takes his hand and gives him a tour, including a turn in Lionel Messi’s chair. They wore matching Inter Miami jerseys, and Beckham’s had “Mr. David” printed on the back. They signed each other’s shirts and went out on the field to score a few goals. View this post on Instagram The family thought that was the whole plan, but there was more. When the players came out of the tunnel before the game, Huddy walked out holding Messi’s hand. View this post on Instagram “We didn’t know that he was going to walk out with Messi,” Droubay said. “We just knew we were going to meet David Beckham and watch a game. (Beckham) went out of his way and orchestrated everything because I think he genuinely just wanted Huddy to have the best experience.” View this post on Instagram Droubay started sharing Huddy’s life online when he was born, on an account just for friends and family. Moments like this one, she said, mean everything. “I want Huddy to grow up knowing that he belongs everywhere, that he’s capable of amazing things, and that having Down syndrome doesn’t limit the joy and opportunities he deserves in life,” she said. View this post on Instagram The post How a young boy’s viral soccer videos led to an unforgettable day with David Beckham and Lionel Messi appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? Reading Time: 5 minutes How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? When you envision a typical construction site, you likely picture roaring diesel engines, towering waste bins and clouds of dust. However, forward-thinking builders are proving that heavy-duty work doesn’t have to create heavy pollution. While traditional operations take a massive toll on the planet through emissions and discarded scrap, you can drive real change on the ground. By embracing thoughtful equipment care, cleaner energy and circular material sourcing, your crews can build a greener world from the ground up. 1. Prioritizing Low-Emissions and Salvaged Materials Every major construction project begins with a blueprint, but the materials you specify in those early drawings dictate your build’s lifetime environmental footprint. Traditional supplies like standard Portland cement and virgin structural steel carry staggering amounts of embodied carbon—the hidden greenhouse gas emissions generated during raw material extraction, manufacturing, and transport. Many firms are swapping out carbon-intensive staples for lower-impact alternatives that still perform reliably. Mass timber, sustainably harvested from certified forests, sequesters atmospheric carbon right inside a building’s frame. Meanwhile, opting for supplementary materials, such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag — a recycled industrial by-product that can replace part of the cement in concrete — can significantly undercut the carbon emissions of traditional concrete mixes. Sustainability also means keeping things local and circular. By sourcing reclaimed lumber, crushed stone and recycled structural steel from regional deconstruction projects, you eliminate the fuel burned shipping heavy freight across the country. Salvaging high-quality elements prevents unnecessary virgin extraction, reduces procurement costs and gives historic materials a useful second life. 2. Adopting Proactive Machinery Maintenance to Reduce Waste and Boost Efficiency A truly sustainable jobsite isn’t just about what’s being built, but also about how efficiently machines run while building it. Proactive heavy equipment care is an essential pillar of low-impact construction. When diesel-powered machinery operates at peak mechanical efficiency, engines encounter less drag, burn significantly less fuel and prevent harmful oil leaks from threatening surrounding soil and local waterways. Routine inspections and precision adjustments prevent premature component breakdowns, keeping bulky metal and synthetic assemblies out of scrap heaps. Daily cleanings with a pressure washer clear away packed dirt and rocks that strain the undercarriage rollers, while maintaining proper track sag prevents engine strain and reduces excess fuel consumption. For example, checking the rubber tracks on skid steers to avoid wear and tear while encouraging optimal performance through proper tension reduces engine strain from overly tight tracks. Doing so means saving fuel and protecting components, leading to fewer emissions and a longer lifespan, which reduces manufacturing footprints. Prioritizing consistent preventive maintenance across excavators and loaders also curbs project delays and saves expenses. 3. Cutting Site Waste Through Circular Construction Practices Traditional construction projects generate mountains of debris, but progressive firms are more often viewing discarded materials as valuable future commodities. Moving toward a circular model begins with systematic on-site sorting, so instead of commingling off-cuts and packaging into generic roll-off dumpster bins, crews establish clearly labeled recovery stations for clean timber, scrap metal, cardboard and masonry. Processing materials directly where the work occurs can save significant hauling fuel and slash disposal tipping fees. Contractors often deploy portable rock crushers to break down clean demo concrete and masonry rubble on-site, producing quality sub-base aggregate to use for access roads, staging areas and sturdy foundation pads. When structures must come down, intentional deconstruction is replacing wrecking balls. Instead of demolishing older framing, crews carefully deconstruct timber and fixtures for repurposing in community projects or donation. Through active partnerships with local salvage yards and regional architectural reclaimers, firms keep large volumes of solid waste out of municipal landfills and help nearby communities access sturdy, character-rich, reusable materials. 4. Cleaning Up Fleet Power Heavy diesel machinery is a core part of commercial construction, but powering an entire fleet on fossil fuels carries a steep environmental and human price tag. Construction vehicles can emit substantial particulate matter and greenhouse gases, worsening local air quality while driving up fuel costs. Consequently, modern contractors are investigating ways to make fleet operations cleaner, quieter and more efficient. Electrification is leading this charge, especially among compact utility machinery. Battery-powered mini-excavators, electric wheel loaders and cordless hand tools deliver instant torque without generating smelly exhaust fumes or extreme noise levels. The shift to electric dramatically improves jobsite air quality, safeguards the respiratory health of on-site crews and earns goodwill from neighboring residential communities. Many larger diesel rigs cannot yet fully transition to electric powertrains, so operational discipline must bridge the sustainability gap. Establishing an automatic five-minute engine shut-off rule for loaders and haul trucks will reduce the exhaust fumes in the air while shaving gallons off daily diesel usage. Routine fuel tracking can ensure every engine runs at peak efficiency. 5. Leveraging Smart Planning and Modular Prefabrication Careful planning can make modern jobsites more efficient, with organized factory processes replacing crowded material storage areas. Modular prefabrication shifts significant building processes off-site into climate-controlled manufacturing facilities. In these organized plant environments, automated cutting systems reduce raw material scrap while optimizing usage down to the millimeter. Assembling wall panels off-site allows workers to recycle off-cuts and minimize on-site construction noise and dust. Simultaneously, modular construction eases neighborhood strain by slashing repetitive truck traffic. Instead of individual supply trucks trickling through local residential streets each day, preassembled building modules arrive in consolidated shipments. Digital project management platforms take this operational efficiency even further with advanced scheduling software accurately tracking incoming deliveries to ensure high-value lumber, drywall and delicate insulation arrive exactly when crews are ready to install them. As a result, there are fewer chaotic staging yards and likely a large reduction in expensive, weather-related material damage from heavy rain or exposure to damp ground. 6. Building a Jobsite Culture Around Everyday Sustainability Advanced equipment and green certifications certainly help, but authentic sustainability ultimately begins with people. Creating an eco-conscious jobsite means fostering a crew culture with daily habits that make resource conservation feel simple and worthwhile. The small decisions made throughout an ordinary shift quickly multiply across multi-month commercial developments. Simple operational swaps, like eliminating disposable water bottles in favor of refillable hydration stations and ditching single-use plastic wrap, drastically curb daily jobsite litter and establish an environmental mindset on the ground. Switching to energy-efficient LED lightbulbs in temporary site offices and encouraging shared crew transit foster an office and field culture in which eco-friendly choices become second nature. Sustainability-minded firms actively show their teams how these practical habits mirror broader everyday eco-friendly lifestyles. Incorporating simple sustainable living ideas into workers’ routines inspires tradespeople to make mindful, low-waste choices at home and at work. When crew members see company leadership genuinely backing these principles, green building becomes a shared source of pride instead of just a compliance task. Lay the Groundwork for a Cleaner Industry You can transform your construction operation into a more sustainable operation without overhauling everything overnight. True sustainability is an ongoing journey built on practical, everyday choices. By making each project cleaner, less wasteful and more efficient, you will make a tangible difference with every build. You hold the power to reshape the building landscape, proving that with each structure, you can construct a stronger, cleaner and more resilient tomorrow. Έχει παρακολουθήσει τη σχέση των ανθρώπων με την κοντινή όχθη του ποταμού να αλλάζει.
