Conclusion A well-planned privacy fence can make a backyard more comfortable, define outdoor spaces, and complement a home’s appearance. By considering materials, layout, maintenance, gates, and budget before installation, homeowners can make informed decisions that fit their property and long-term needs. 326 Fence Construction provides custom fencing solutions throughout Collin County and surrounding North Texas communities, helping property owners explore practical options for their fencing projects. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Reducing Waste in Renovation Projects Can Be Easy: Just Apply These 7 Practices Reading Time: 4 minutes Reducing Waste in Renovation Projects Can Be Easy: Just Apply These 7 Practices Renovating your home can leave behind more waste than you might expect. Old cabinets, broken tiles, discarded flooring, leftover paint and piles of packaging can quickly add up. Much of this material ends up in landfills, even though some could have been reused, donated or recycled. However, a few changes in how you plan, shop and manage construction waste can make your renovation more sustainable and keep useful materials in circulation. Here are seven ways to reduce waste in your home renovation projects. 1. Plan Your Renovation Before Buying Materials Your renovation might involve just one room, but the materials you use still contribute to the construction industry’s environmental footprint. The buildings and construction sector contributes to 37% of global emissions and nearly 50% of global material extraction. You can reduce the resources your project consumes, including materials that might otherwise end up unused, by planning your renovation carefully. Before placing orders, measure each room and calculate how much flooring, paint and lumber you’ll need. Ask your contractor to help estimate quantities, accounting for reasonable cutting allowances and possible mistakes. This gives you a better shopping list and helps prevent excessive purchases. Design decisions are equally important. Finalize flooring, wall finish and cabinet style choices before construction begins. Changing these halfway through the project can leave you with surplus materials that no longer suit your plans. Coordination between you, your contractor and suppliers can keep purchasing on track. 2. Keep Existing Materials and Fixtures Where Possible Your home’s existing features might have plenty of life left in them. Keeping functional materials in place reduces the need for new products, which require raw materials and energy to manufacture and deliver. Take a good look at your cabinets, doors, flooring, countertops and plumbing fixtures before deciding what needs replacing. For example, a garage door with a standard torsion spring may last around 10,000 operating cycles. If it still works and its components are in good condition, regular maintenance could extend its useful lifespan. You can refresh outdated features with simple updates. Repaint kitchen cabinets, swap old handles, refinish hardwood floors or replace the bathroom vanity’s faucet. These changes can make familiar features look new again while keeping bulky materials out of the waste pile. Even retaining existing structural elements can prevent substantial demolition waste. 3. Choose Reclaimed and Recycled Building Materials Keeping existing building materials is a good start, but you can make your shopping list even more sustainable by choosing reclaimed and recycled products. They keep existing resources in circulation and reduce the need to extract and process additional raw materials. Look for reclaimed timber, salvaged bricks, recycled glass countertops, recycled metal fixtures and flooring made with recycled content. Architectural salvage yards and secondhand building supply stores are great places to explore. You might even find distinctive pieces that add character to your home, such as an old wooden door or vintage light fixture. Check the condition, safety and suitability of each material before purchasing. Reclaimed wood, for example, should be inspected for rot, pests and damage. You should also make sure recycled products meet the requirements for their intended use. 4. Store Leftover Materials for Future Repairs Extra tiles, flooring planks and paint cans could come in handy long after your renovation is finished. Keeping useful leftovers gives you matching materials for future projects, so you can replace a damaged section without purchasing an entirely new batch. Set aside spare tiles, grout, screws, cabinet handles, paint and flooring pieces. Keep them in their original packaging where possible and label everything clearly. Follow storage instructions carefully because products such as paint and adhesives may need specific temperature conditions. You may also need a place to store these supplies while construction is underway. A portable storage unit can hold renovation materials and other belongings away from busy work areas. It may also protect furniture and household items from dust and debris during renovation, reducing the risk of damage to your belongings. 5. Work With Contractors Who Prioritize Waste Reduction Your contractor has a big influence on how much waste your renovation produces. Their choices around demolition, material ordering and waste disposal can determine whether usable items are salvaged or thrown away. Before hiring someone, ask about their approach to construction waste . Do they separate recyclable materials? Can they carefully remove existing fixtures for reuse? Do they work with local recycling facilities or salvage organizations? These questions can help you understand how they handle unwanted materials. Discuss your waste reduction goals before work begins and agree on practical arrangements for sorting, collecting and disposing of debris. You can also ask contractors to track leftover materials and avoid unnecessary purchases. Clear communication helps everyone work toward the same goal. 6. Donate, Sell or Reuse Items That Are Still in Good Condition Some materials removed during your renovation could be useful in another home or construction project. Donating or selling them gives these items another purpose and reduces the demand for newly manufactured products. The EPA points out that reducing landfill waste can offset the environmental toll of mining raw materials and making new items from scratch. Look for easy-to-remove items such as doors, appliances and fixtures. You can offer them to local charities, secondhand building supply stores or people working on their own renovation projects. Working appliances and attractive light fixtures may also find buyers through online marketplaces. Other leftover materials can serve different purposes. Wood cutoffs can become smaller framing pieces, blocking or garden mulch. You can reuse crushed brick, masonry and concrete as fill, road base or driveway bedding. Even leftover paint can be remixed for use in storage rooms and garages, or used as a primer on another project. Before donating or repurposing the item, ensure its condition is suitable. 7. Reduce Packaging and Avoid Single-Use Supplies Renovation waste doesn’t come exclusively from construction materials. Cardboard boxes, plastic wrapping, protective films and disposable supplies can create another pile of trash before the actual work is finished. Ask suppliers about bulk ordering, minimal packaging and reusable delivery containers. You can also coordinate deliveries so materials arrive in fewer shipments, reducing excess packaging and transportation needs. Save sturdy cardboard boxes and packing materials to organize supplies or protect furniture during construction. For the renovation itself, choose reusable drop cloths, protective coverings and storage containers where practical. Washable cloths can replace disposable plastic sheets for many jobs, while reusable buckets and organizers can serve you throughout the project. Small changes to your purchasing and cleanup habits can prevent a surprising amount of waste. A Renovation That Doesn’t Cost the Earth A beautiful home and a lighter environmental footprint can go hand in hand. With some careful planning, material reuse and smarter waste management, you can make your renovation more sustainable at every stage. You might even find unique materials and creative ways to refresh your space along the way. Make your next home makeover one that looks good and wastes fewer resources. The post Reducing Waste in Renovation Projects Can Be Easy: Just Apply These 7 Practices appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Commonplace moments with a stranger can make all the difference in helping someone feel like they belong. You’re walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You’re tired, you’re leaving without the produce you came for, and you’re embarrassed. You pass by an older woman on the way out, steeling yourself for judgment. Instead, you get a knowing smile and hear, “We’ve all been there. You’re doing great, Mama.” And suddenly, you feel seen. Until recently, these sparks of connection didn’t have a name. Now, thanks to a University of Georgia researcher, they do: evanescent interactions. “What is communicated by these evanescent interactions is essentially, ‘You’ve noticed me. You’ve confirmed my existence. You’ve communicated that I am welcome here, that I belong here, that I have a place here, that I have value,'” says Joseph Hermanowicz, author of the publication and a professor of sociology at the University of Georgia. Hermanowicz defines evanescent interactions as brief moments when “strangers exchange gestures that create a ‘spark’ between them.” An evanescent interaction is more than just an ordinary exchange of pleasantries. These moments consist of brief but meaningful exchanges of mutual understanding and connection. “It’s important to be pleasant and kind to people, particularly in our present times, of course,” Hermanowicz says. “But I think it’s also important to recognize that when we do have a certain deliberateness with communicating with people, we could be accomplishing something very meaningful. We could communicate to people that they are important, that they matter, that we together form a community.” In his earlier research on the causes of undergraduate attrition, Hermanowicz found that evanescent interactions often influenced whether a student stuck it out or dropped out. Former students who dropped out says that a meaningful encounter with someone at the university who showed genuine interest in their well-being might have helped them feel more like they belonged. “In the absence of such contact, they felt alienated and not noticed, which fueled or did not impede a desire to leave,” he says. “So they left. “A lot of people are lonely. These sparks of connection can thwart feelings of not belonging in the various groups and organizations that we are a part of, whether those are friendship groups, work organizations, or society more broadly.” Evanescent interactions are brief, positive, and highly emotionally charged. They’re so ordinary that people may not give them a second thought. But they hold larger significance, Hermanowicz says. “Evanescent interactions are crucial to social life,” he says. “Two people communicating empathy to each other and recognizing each other as important holds extraordinary consequence. It affirms our mutual place in human community.” The article appears in Theory and Society . Source: University of Georgia The post How connecting with strangers can boost the sense of belonging appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: There was a time when Gouthami Ravi and Sharan Kulkarni would have given anything to hear their daughter cry. Today, in their Bengaluru home, one-year-old Chikoo fills their days with little sounds, playful movements and the curiosity of a child discovering the world around her. She plays on the bed, makes her presence felt and gives her parents the kind of ordinary moments they once could only hope for. For months, they had watched over her breathing, learnt to manage medical equipment, and prepared for emergencies. A tracheostomy tube in her throat meant they could no longer hear her cry. Their home had become a medical care unit, and every day revolved around keeping their little girl safe. On 10 March 2026, after months of treatment, Chikoo's tracheostomy was finally removed. Sharan remembers that even before the procedure, he had held on to a belief that his daughter would survive. "We were not in a dilemma that it was 50-50 always. It was always 100%. She's going to survive," he says. That conviction carried the couple through a premature birth, frightening medical emergencies and months of round-the-clock care. But their experience also left them with a desire to help other families facing a similar journey. Born seven weeks premature, Chikoo weighed just 2.05 kg and needed breathing support soon after birth. When Chikoo needed a tracheostomy at barely a month old, they searched online for Indian parents who had been through the same experience. They found very little that could prepare them for what lay ahead. "I am so alone in this journey," Sharan remembers feeling. Today, Gouthami and Sharan want to make sure other parents facing a similar situation do not have to navigate it without guidance. They are open to speaking directly with families whose children may need a tracheostomy, sharing what they learnt through Chikoo's treatment and helping them understand what to expect. This includes practical guidance on questions to ask doctors, preparing a home for a child with a tracheostomy, learning tube changes and understanding how to respond to emergencies. They also want to be open about the medical, emotional and financial demands of long-term care, so families have a clearer picture of what lies ahead. While every child's medical needs are different and decisions must be made with the treating doctors, Gouthami and Sharan hope that sharing their experience can help another family feel less alone and better prepared. A premature birth, followed by an unexpected crisis Chikoo was born on 2 September 2025, seven weeks before her expected due date. Weighing just 2.05 kg, she needed breathing support and was moved to a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) soon after birth. A stomach infection added to her early medical challenges. After around 15 days of treatment, she was discharged. Her parents brought her home, believing that the difficult beginning was behind them. "We thought it was the same way," Gouthami recalls, explaining how they assumed their daughter had recovered as many babies do after a NICU stay. They began settling into the routines of caring for a newborn: feeding, bathing, and looking after their little girl. Then, about a month into her life, something frightening happened. Chikoo's parents learnt to manage her tracheostomy care at home, from handling medical equipment to preparing for emergencies. During a feed, Chikoo began choking. Her skin turned blue, and she became unresponsive. Gouthami, who knew CPR, tried to help her while the family rushed to the hospital. Chikoo eventually began breathing again, and her oxygen levels appeared normal when they arrived. The family was sent home, with the episode attributed to a feeding issue. But when the same thing happened again about a week later, Gouthami and Sharan knew something was wrong. This time, Chikoo's oxygen levels began falling, and she needed sustained respiratory support. Further investigations revealed a combination of airway conditions, including laryngomalacia, a laryngeal cleft and tongue-base obstruction. Together, these were affecting her ability to coordinate feeding and breathing safely. The couple had entered a world of medical terminology, hospital admissions and decisions they had never imagined making for their newborn. The decision that changed everything As they began navigating unfamiliar diagnoses and difficult treatment decisions, the family relied on the guidance of their medical team. Gouthami and Sharan are grateful to Dr Sudheer K A, Dr Srikanta J T, Dr Antony George and Dr Priyanka Potti, Dr Vikas Satwik and Dr Sneha Lingappa, and Dr Shwetha Anand Baratikke from the pulmonary, paediatric, and gynaecology departments. The family credits the doctors involved in Chikoo's care for helping them navigate a period filled with uncertainty and decisions they had never expected to make. Gouthami and Sharan spent months learning the practical aspects of tracheostomy care so they could look after their daughter safely at home. As Chikoo continued to need breathing support, doctors recommended a tracheostomy, a procedure in which an opening is made in the neck to provide an airway through a tube. For a baby barely a month old, it was an overwhelming prospect. The first attempt was unsuccessful. The family had already been through the fear of watching their daughter struggle to breathe and the weight of agreeing to a major procedure. Now, they had to find the strength to try again. The second tracheostomy, performed in October 2025, was successful. But the procedure was only the beginning of another demanding phase. Chikoo needed time to recover and gradually come off the ventilator and oxygen support. Her parents spent weeks waiting outside the NICU, looking for updates and hoping that each day would bring progress. "Emotionally, we were too down," Gouthami says, describing what the family went through. With a suction machine, pulse oximeter and feeding pump at home, the family adapted their everyday routines to meet Chikoo's medical needs. They were also thinking about Chikoo's future. Gouthami wanted to understand whether her daughter would be able to develop and live as other children did. The family sought medical assessments, including checks on her neurological responses, and held on to the reassurance that these results offered. For Sharan, the answer was to keep believing in his daughter , even when the outcome was uncertain. "I never asked God for anything else," he says, describing how he imagined a future in which Chikoo would grow up and experience life beyond the hospital. That belief did not make the difficult days disappear. It gave them something to hold on to as they navigated one decision at a time. When home became a medical care unit After months of hospital care, Chikoo was eventually able to return home with her tracheostomy in place. But bringing her home did not mean returning to normal life. The family had to prepare their house for her medical needs, arranging equipment such as a suction machine, a pulse oximeter and a feeding pump. They also changed their daily routines to reduce potential irritants in the air. With nurses working in shifts, Gouthami and Sharan ensured Chikoo received the care and attention she needed at home. For months, they avoided lighting incense and made special arrangements for cooking. Nurses cared for Chikoo in shifts, with a dedicated space arranged for them at home. Yet Gouthami and Sharan knew that professional help could not always be immediately available. They therefore underwent practical training to learn how to care for the tracheostomy and respond to emergencies. "We had a booklet given. We had to read through that, do the Google research and go back the next day and explain what it is about," Gouthami recalls. The training lasted around 20 days. They learnt the procedures, familiarised themselves with the equipment and prepared themselves to manage situations that could arise at home. Learning to care for Chikoo at home also meant learning to trust their own hands while knowing when to seek medical help. The couple remains grateful to the medical team for guiding them through the practical aspects of her care and helping them prepare for emergencies. Their home nurses, Amina Ajusha and Aditya Sivadas, were also part of the support system that helped the family manage Chikoo's daily needs. Every 15 days, the family travelled back to the hospital for a tracheostomy tube change, carrying the equipment Chikoo depended on. They also had to learn how to perform the change themselves under medical supervision, knowing that they might need to act in an emergency. From monitoring her breathing to managing medical equipment, Chikoo's home-care routine required constant attention and coordination. Work had to find its place around these responsibilities. Gouthami was able to draw on maternity leave, while Sharan reorganised his business so that much of his work could be managed from home. His team supported him, allowing him to attend to his daughter while keeping the business running. The couple also leaned heavily on their families. "The need for having parents at home is extremely important," Sharan says. "Even today, without them, we cannot stay at home even one day." Gouthami credits her employer, SAP, for supporting her through this period. "SAP stood by me like family. The medical insurance and mental-health support gave me the confidence to make financial decisions for my daughter's care. I am endlessly thankful to my company for being there for me when I needed that support the most," she says. Chikoo's nurses became an important part of the support system that helped the family navigate life after her hospital discharge. The financial demands of Chikoo's treatment were considerable. From her hospital care and medical procedures to the home-care arrangements she needed until her tracheostomy was removed, the family spent approximately Rs 35 lakh. The family's personal health insurance covered only a part of the total expense, leaving them to manage the remaining costs alongside the demands of her care. The day they heard her voice again For months, Chikoo's parents had been unable to hear her cry with the tracheostomy in place. Before the tube could be removed, she underwent a series of carefully monitored steps, including a speech-valve trial and a capping trial to assess her ability to breathe through her nose and mouth. For Gouthami and Sharan, hearing Chikoo cry again was an emotional moment after months of being unable to hear her voice because of the tracheostomy tube. The process required patience. Chikoo did not immediately tolerate every step, and there were moments when the family had to wait longer than expected. Rather than rushing, they followed the medical team's guidance and gave her the time she needed. Then came a moment they had been waiting for. "When we were cleaning the tracheostomy, she started crying, and we could hear her voice," Sharan recalls. It was a sound that meant far more than words could express. The family and the nurses who had cared for Chikoo were moved to tears. After the trials and necessary medical assessments, her tracheostomy was permanently removed on 10 March 2026. Sharan remembers that no words could describe the moment. They went to the doctor and thanked the medical team. Looking back, he says, "It is not about being right here. It is about taking the next step." Today, Chikoo attends daycare, plays with toys and spends her days exploring new experiences as her parents watch her grow. Today, watching Chikoo play, vocalise, and grow, they can see how far she has come. She now goes to daycare, where she spends her days surrounded by bright toys, new little friends and plenty of activity. While a few developmental milestones are still catching up, her parents describe her as curious, energetic, and full of life. The medical equipment and routines that once dominated their lives no longer define every moment of their daughter's day. If you are a parent looking to connect with Gouthami and Sharan, you can reach out to The Better India team for their contact details or connect with them directly through their Instagram accounts. All images courtesy of Gouthami and Sharan.

items.descriptionOriginal: Every geological epoch leaves signatures. One of the Anthropocene’s may be a noise. Oceans echo with the drone of ship engines and blasts of sonar. Cities and suburbs roar with speeding cars and revving motorcycles. Even remote wilderness hums with passing airplanes and strolling hikers. Humanity has turned up the volume on the whole planet. That soundtrack is far reaching. New research in Science finds that noise pollution more than doubles death rates among wild animals. It is also rewriting the rules of who eats whom. In noisy places, prey grow jumpy and predators go hungry. Sometimes an animal fleeing the din runs straight into danger. Noise, the authors write, “reshapes the acoustic arms race” between species, and it creates winners and losers. The researchers argue that protecting wildlife in the Anthropocene means protecting quiet. “This work shows that noise pollution is an underrated threat to wildlife worldwide,” said Hansjoerg Kunc , an ecologist at Queen’s University Belfast and the paper’s lead author. Soundscapes, he said, should be safeguarded with the same seriousness as forests, wetlands and other physical habitats. Scientists have long known that noise harms living things. The World Health Organization calls it a serious health hazard for people: it shortens lives, impairs children’s brain development and disrupts sleep. In wildlife, noise has been shown to spike stress hormones in freshwater fish, alter feeding behavior , and cause forest dwellers to flee in panic . .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby What was missing was the big picture. Kunc and Queen’s colleague Rouven Schmidt gathered 214 studies examining noise effects on 177 species across six continents, from tiny beetles to hulking whales. They focused on controlled experiments, which can more reliably pin effects on noise itself. The effects were widespread. Noise was tied to fetal deformities, weakened immune systems and elevated stress hormones. It altered body size, feeding and parenting, and it changed animals’ success at hunting or escaping hunters. Pooled across the experiments, noise raised mortality by 138%. If 10 in every 100 animals would die in a world without human noise, 24 would die in a world with it. That’s large enough, the authors say, to “threaten population viability.” The effects on how species interact may matter just as much. Animals tended to steer clear of noisy areas, so their numbers there were 37% lower. The prey that remained were on high alert. So predators in noisy places caught 25% less prey, even though they worked harder to find it. But noise doesn’t necessarily help prey either. A loud sound might send a prey animal into a burrow or other enclosed space to hide. Those close quarters can amplify the noise, and that can flush the animal back into the open, where a predator is waiting. The fix, the researchers suggest, starts with treating sound as part of habitat. Kunc points to “measures such as low-noise zones that give animals a genuine acoustic refuge.” In an epoch defined by human influence, quiet may be one of the habitats most worth saving. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News FireSat Satellites Begin Delivering Twice-Daily Wildfire Data Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes FireSat, a satellite constellation built for wildfire detection, launched its first operational satellites in July 2026 and began delivering twice-daily fire data worldwide. FireSat, a satellite constellation built specifically to spot wildfires, reached orbit for the first time as an operational system in July 2026. SpaceX launched three satellites from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California aboard a SpaceX rocket. Within two hours, all three had established contact with ground teams, marking the system’s shift from demonstration to active service. The constellation comes from Earth Fire Alliance , a nonprofit coalition built around a single goal: catching wildfires earlier than existing satellites can. Most space-based fire detection today relies on instruments designed for weather or general Earth observation. FireSat was engineered from the ground up for one job, drawing on interviews with more than 200 firefighters, incident commanders, and scientists worldwide. That focus shows up in the hardware. FireSat’s sensors can detect a fire as small as five meters by five meters, roughly the size of two parking spaces. Six imaging channels across five spectral bands work together to separate real fires from false alarms, keeping the error rate under five percent. A second midwave infrared channel addresses a specific technical problem. A single sensor can essentially overexpose when pointed at an extremely hot fire, much like a camera struggles with a bright light source. The extra channel is tuned to stay accurate even at the highest temperatures. These three satellites currently revisit the world’s most fire-prone regions at least twice daily. Earth Fire Alliance plans to shrink that gap to about one hour by 2029 as more satellites join the constellation. A full build-out of more than 50 satellites, targeted for 2030, would bring worldwide revisit times down to 20 minutes or less. Early results are already circulating. In September 2026, the team released its first active-fire images from the operational satellites, captured roughly three weeks after launch. Earlier tests with a single demonstration satellite had already caught a small roadside fire in Oregon that existing systems missed entirely. That demonstration satellite, launched in March 2025, spent more than a year in orbit proving the sensor technology before the operational constellation followed. During that period, it also captured thermal activity unrelated to wildfires, including a volcanic eruption and gas flares at an oil field, showing the instrument could distinguish between different types of heat sources. Those early tests gave engineers confidence to move from a single prototype to a working constellation. A wildfire burns through forested terrain at dusk, the kind of early-stage blaze FireSat is designed to catch before it spreads. Photo by Pixabay on Pexels. Beyond raw detection, FireSat tracks how a fire grows and moves once it starts. Data on a fire’s perimeter, spread direction, and radiative power feeds directly into incident commanders’ decisions. That kind of detail can shape evacuation orders and help responders decide where to send limited crews and equipment. Faster detection also offers a real cost benefit. Published research suggests that a one-hour revisit rate across the United States alone could help avoid more than a billion dollars in fire damage annually. Projections also point to roughly 3,500 homes protected and 21.9 million tons of carbon emissions prevented each year once the system reaches that pace. The project has been funded by a mix of philanthropic and corporate backers, including the Bezos Earth Fund, Google.org, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation. Fire agencies such as CAL FIRE and research partners, including the Environmental Defense Fund, joined an early adopter program to help shape how the data is delivered. That early input helped earn the project a TIME Best Invention of 2025. Access to the data remains a central question as the system scales up. According to Earth Fire Alliance, the goal is to make FireSat data available to any fire agency, scientist, or community that needs it, not only wealthy nations with existing satellite programs. Whether that goal holds up as the constellation grows will shape how evenly its benefits reach fire-prone regions worldwide. For now, three satellites mark the start of what Earth Fire Alliance hopes becomes a global, persistent eye on wildfire . As more FireSat satellites join orbit over the coming years, the gap between a fire’s first spark and the moment responders learn about it should keep shrinking. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Who Gets to Protect the Ocean? Coral Catch is Expanding the Circle of Marine Conservation Reading Time: 3 minutes In Indonesia, Coral Catch is helping women gain the skills, confidence, and opportunities to become divers, researchers, educators, and leaders in marine conservation. Marine conservation is often measured in numbers: corals planted, reef area restored, biodiversity returning. Those numbers matter, and Coral Catch tracks them closely. But as the Indonesian nonprofit’s work grew, so did a different question: who gets the opportunity to protect these ecosystems? Coral Catch began in Indonesia’s Gili Matra Marine Protected Area with a focus on coral restoration. Over time, the team saw that its impact was reaching beyond the restoration sites. Women were growing more confident underwater, pursuing roles in marine conservation and research that once felt out of reach, and finding opportunities to become educators, advocates, and mentors. As more women moved through the program, these individual experiences began to form something larger: a pathway into marine conservation that connects training and diving opportunities with research, restoration, community engagement, and professional development. Coral Catch began to see that its impact was not only about how much reef it could restore, but also about who had the opportunity to become an ocean protector and what could happen when that opportunity continued beyond the initial training. Tania’s experience is one example of what that pathway can make possible. She grew up in Tangerang, a city far from the ocean, and arrived on Gili Air in January 2025 determined to become a marine researcher. Over nine weeks, she trained as a diver and graduated as a scientific diver, gaining not only technical skills but also the confidence to pursue a place in marine conservation. Today, Tania leads shark research in the Gili Matra Marine Protected Area, studying how tourism affects white-tip reef sharks using underwater cameras and acoustic monitoring. She has secured her own research grant and now mentors new Coral Catch participants, becoming part of the same network that helped her move forward. Cenna’s experience reflects another side of the access challenge. Growing up in Surabaya, she saw diving as something women around her did not commonly pursue. At university, she joined a diving club and loved being underwater, but field positions often required experience she had not yet had the opportunity to gain. In 2022, an online talk by a Coral Catch alumna showed Cenna that marine conservation could be a path for her too. She joined Coral Catch’s second group of participants and later worked in sustainable fisheries and community development. Today, she is Coral Catch’s Project and Partnerships Manager, supporting the program and the women coming through it. A Coral Catch Superwoman shares marine conservation lessons with local schoolchildren, extending the program’s reach far beyond the reef. Photo courtesy of Coral Catch Their journeys are now part of a much larger network. Coral Catch has trained 44 Indonesian women, with around 50% progressing to professional-level diving qualifications, and the organization aims to reach 100 women by 2030. Many alumni continue working in marine conservation or sustainable tourism, sharing what they know with their communities, returning to Coral Catch as mentors or taking on new roles, and becoming examples for younger women who may not have previously seen themselves in conservation. This network is central to how Coral Catch approaches conservation. Through its Academy and other programs, participants can move from learning and hands-on training into research, restoration, community engagement, and professional opportunities. The goal is not simply to provide access to the ocean, but to create pathways that allow people to build skills and continue contributing long after their initial training. That approach matters because access to marine conservation is not equal. Through its work, Coral Catch has seen women face barriers to marine education, diving, field experience, and conservation careers. At the same time, coral reefs support livelihoods, food security, tourism, and coastal protection, making the health of these ecosystems closely connected to the communities around them. Coral Catch’s work therefore extends beyond its training programs. The Gili Dive Club gives local community members access to diving and marine conservation training every Sunday, creating another entry point for people who want to develop practical skills and become involved in protecting their local marine environment. Coral Catch also organizes conservation expeditions twice a year, giving participants opportunities to turn travel into meaningful, hands-on experiences in marine conservation. The same approach is now being explored beyond Indonesia. Through its collaboration with Universiti Malaysia Terengganu, Coral Catch is looking at how lessons and approaches developed through its work in Indonesia can be adapted to support women and coastal communities in a different regional context. That does not mean simply copying the Indonesian model. Malaysia has its own cultural, ecological, and institutional context, so Coral Catch is working with local partners and listening to what communities and women there need. What carries forward is the broader foundation of conservation, empowerment, local capacity building, and community ownership. For Coral Catch, restoring reefs remains essential. But conservation is also about creating the people and pathways needed to sustain that work. When women have access to training, field experience, research, mentorship, and professional opportunities, they can become not just participants in conservation, but divers, researchers, educators, mentors, and leaders shaping the future of the world’s oceans. items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. In the bag A low-cost, low-tech intervention is saving lives in maternity wards across Africa. As the New York Times reports in a story shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas, the maternal drape is a plastic pouch that can be used to easily measure blood loss. This allows health workers to act quickly in the case of postpartum hemorrhage, which is extremely dangerous. When combined with the necessary treatments, this intervention cut deaths by postpartum hemorrhage by about two-thirds. “The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite,” Dr. Hadiza Galadanci, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Bayero University in Kano, Nigeria, told the Times . “It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems.” Michaela says: I had no idea a simple, low-cost plastic bag is saving so many mothers’ lives. Bird’s-eye view In a lighter (but just as surprising) story of lives being saved, googly-eyed buoys are helping prevent seabirds from getting caught in fishing nets. According to a Mongabay story that caught the attention of Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, these devices scare the birds away from the fishing gear. A study off Cornwall, England, found that nets fitted with kites shaped like birds of prey had 71 percent lower odds of catching seabirds, and nets with spinning “looming-eye” buoys had 59 percent lower odds. Becca says: I kinda love these “googly-eyed buoys,” despite their uncanny resemblance to Clippy the paperclip . What else we’re reading The fix for America’s terrible internet is hiding in Tennessee — shared by RTBC Founder David Byrne from Vox What If a Crisis Pregnancy Center Was Pro-Choice? — shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby from The Cut The planet’s vital signs are getting worse. One of the easiest fixes is your diet. — shared by Michaela Haas from Grist In other news… Just after last week’s historic midterm elections, we wrapped up The Depolarization Series , an exploration of the many ways people are defying division and really listening to those who disagree with them. You can check out the full series here — and don’t miss the many fantastic videos we shared on Instagram. items.descriptionOriginal: In Fargo, North Dakota, Prakash Mathew and his wife Jane had a beautiful garden people would often stop to admire. They made a point of writing down their visitors' names and would greet each by name the next time. Over time, they provided extra chairs and invited people to sit and chat, and a different kind of garden emerged. "When we went for our walks, we could hardly walk two blocks without stopping and talking to someone." Jane died suddenly in December of last year. When summer came, Prakash continued to go to the driveway, and people still joined him. He asked, "What if we did this — sat in my driveway, but intentionally, every other week, with a topic?" Everybody loved it. Driveway Dialogues was born. A neighborhood spirit had been planted, "with a garden, a few extra chairs in front of the house, and a curiosity to care for others."

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Electric School Buses are Cutting Charging Costs in New York City Reading Time: 3 minutes Electric school buses now serve New York City students, and a trenchless charging method cut construction costs by 13%. Electric school buses now carry students across Brooklyn and Queens. First Student and Con Edison, the local utility, finished the first phase of this project . It serves the New York City Department of Education. The charging setup is what sets this project apart. First Student built its First Charge system without traditional underground trenching. That choice cut infrastructure construction costs by 13%. Trenching means digging long ditches to bury cables. That work takes time and disrupts daily life in a crowded city. Skipping it simplifies construction and helps buses reach students sooner. Here is a simple way to picture it. For every $100 a traditional installation would cost, the project saved about $13. Those savings help a fleet that needs many chargers for its electric school buses. First Charge is an above-ground system designed by bus operators, for bus operators. It is modular, meaning its parts fit together, and it can grow with a fleet. Con Edison adds that crews did not need to bury the service line to the chargers. A service line is the cable that brings power to a site. The utility says other fleet owners can copy this idea to save money and finish projects faster. Vicki Kuo, a Con Edison senior vice president, says the utility wants electric vehicles to be affordable. Lower upfront costs help make that goal real. Outside funding also helped. Con Edison and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) contributed money to the project. That included six bus vouchers and funding for four retrofit buses, which are existing buses converted to electric power. First Student also helps school districts find funding for electric school buses. Since 2023, it has secured millions of dollars in Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) funding for customers. The buses also charge on a schedule that saves money. Load management software sets charging for off-peak hours. Those are times when fewer people use power and energy costs less. The project also includes bi-directional charging technology. This allows electricity to flow both into and out of a battery. Partners are also exploring more ways to lower energy costs for fleets. Electric school buses in this project use bi-directional charging technology that lets electricity flow both into and out of a battery, while partners explore more ways to lower energy costs for fleets. Photo courtesy of First Student . Kevin Matthews, head of electrification at First Student, says scaling up electric school buses takes more than vehicles. Fleets also need the right chargers, technology, and a strong utility partner. Costs vary by district. First Student says Type C and Type D electric school buses cost around $375,000 each. Its analysis shows lifetime ownership costs matching diesel buses by 2029. Cold weather affects electric school bus range. First Student’s Quebec buses travel 80 to 90 miles per charge, or about 70 in deep cold. Newer, larger batteries reach 100 to 120 miles. Maintenance may get easier too. First Student sees fewer fluids to manage and far fewer brake problems. Fewer moving parts also cut repair time. Electric school buses offer a healthier, quieter ride. Con Edison notes the new buses produce no tailpipe emissions, which means no exhaust from the vehicle itself. They replace less efficient buses that burn fossil fuels. During the 2025-26 school year, First Student ran about 490 electric school buses. More than 550 more are on order. Its electric buses have driven over 11.2 million miles, about 450 trips around the Earth. First Student also runs a fleet of more than 48,000 vehicles across the U.S. and Canada. It carries millions of students each day. That reach means lessons from New York can travel far. Next up are 40 more electric school buses for the New York City Department of Education. First Student is also considering expanded solar use and a smart energy hub at its Brooklyn facilities. Transit agencies nationwide are also learning how electric buses can drive change. Cleaner buses can lower tailpipe pollution on every route. Could electric school buses roll out faster in other cities? First Student and Con Edison say the model can help other fleets overcome cost and construction hurdles. For students in Brooklyn and Queens, the payoff is a quieter ride on a cleaner bus. The post How Electric School Buses are Cutting Charging Costs in New York City appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν ένα γιγάντιο τρωκτικό 66 λιβρών που έζησε πριν από 34 εκατομμύρια χρόνια
items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν απολιθώματα ενός γιγαντιαίου τρωκτικού που έζησε στην Ταϊλάνδη πριν από 34 εκατομμύρια χρόνια, αποκαλύπτοντας ότι τεράστια τρωκτικά εξελίχθηκαν πολύ νωρίτερα από ό,τι πιστεύαμε. Ονομάστηκε Yakamys sirindhornae, το αρχαίο ζώο μπορεί να ζύγιζε περίπου 66 κιλά, περίπου δύο φορές περισσότερο από άλλα γνωστά τρωκτικά της εποχής του.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

items.descriptionOriginal: The year I turned 30, I moved to a peaceful neighborhood on Los Angeles’ Westside. I was 10 minutes from Venice Beach and had an apartment all to myself. The only catch (besides street parking)? It was 450 square feet. A couple of friends helped me optimize the place: We assembled a custom Murphy bed, installed a wall-mounted folding table, and chose decor that made it feel joyful and airy. Though I lamented not having more space at times, I discovered that my scaled-down quarters came with some perks. Styling the studio so intentionally felt empowering, and because it was so small, I often enjoyed my meals out in the courtyard under the sun. Years later, despite having married and moved into a comfortable condo, I still occasionally yearn for more square footage, particularly during dinner parties or when family visits for the holidays. To refresh my perspective, I spoke to interior design experts and therapists who helped illuminate some of the unexpected benefits of having a smaller home — and offered tips for making the most of yours. Benefits domin_domin—iStock/Getty Images Plus Cost and Cleaning We’ll start with perhaps the most obvious but still occasionally overlooked perks: “Less square footage means less time cleaning and organizing. Owning less means spending less time managing and maintaining your belongings,” Phoenix-based interior designer Mackenzie Collier explained in an email to Nice News. “That frees up more time for hobbies, socializing, and anything else you’d rather be doing!” She added that smaller spaces force us to be more thoughtful about what we buy and why (a welcome mindset shift for many), and that the money we save on quantity can be used to invest in quality — e.g., well-built furniture, bespoke decor, art. And it’s not just our shopping carts that feel the difference, Sierra Troitsky , an interior designer in Indianapolis, pointed out. “Smaller spaces are often more economical and environmentally friendly as they cost less to heat and cool,” she said. Mental Well-Being Less square footage can contribute to a greater sense of well-being because it can encourage us to be neat and organized, “which is calming for the brain,” said Sipora Weissman , a licensed therapist in Ventura, California. In a tiny room, a pile of unfolded laundry is a lot more noticeable than in a large one, for example, so we may be more inclined to actually, you know, put it away . “As a therapist who works with adults who get overstimulated easily, living in a small space can be overwhelming or it can actually be very supportive to someone’s nervous system,” Weissman explained. “If you fill that small space with tchotchkes and clutter, that will be a recipe for an unsettled brain. There are many scientific studies that show the negative impacts of clutter on the brain. But if you take this small space living situation as an opportunity, it can be very conducive to your mental health.” More Intentional Decor Just as I experienced when decorating my tiny quarters, less to work with can have a focusing effect. “A small living room lends itself to intentional decorating because you’re forced to narrow in on fewer, impactful pieces that set the tone for the space — say, a beautiful sofa, a well-sized rug, task and accent lighting, and some meaningful artwork,” said Elena Navarro, an interior designer and professional organizer at Sparkly Maid Austin . View this post on Instagram She added: “I love that limited square footage forces you to really think through everything that you bring in the door, from new dishes to cozy throw blankets to holiday decor. Where is the item going to live? Do you use it enough to warrant giving it a permanent home?” Better for Gathering and Bonding The reason celebrity chef Ina Garten considers six people the ideal number for a dinner party is the same reason your modest home might lend itself to more meaningful gatherings: intimacy. “Small group events tend to produce an environment that allows for more personalized conversation,” explained Whitney Willborn , a Texas-based licensed clinical social worker, adding that it’s easier to not only include everyone in the conversation but also to spot when others appear to be excluded. If guests are spread out in different rooms or fragmented into groups, it’s trickier to notice when a new friend is standing awkwardly by themself, for example. Your own family might benefit from a smaller floor plan, too. Collier recently moved out of a 900-square-foot home, and her household has experienced some nostalgia for the cozier living situation. “There was nowhere to escape to, so we’d sit together, watch a movie, or play games,” she said. “Those shared moments became some of our favorite memories.” Spend More Time in Community My al fresco dining habit of yore highlights how the wide world can beckon when your indoors isn’t vast. Collier had the same experience. “I’ve found that living in a small space encourages me to spend more time outdoors and in my community,” she shared. “Whether it was tending to my garden, or heading to a local coffee shop to work, living small naturally pushed me to get out into the community more.” Tips Double Duty Interior designer Preeti Shah made her name in New York, where minuscule apartments are no big deal (one of the tiniest is an infinitesimal 55 square feet !). When she moved to an area of Houston filled with massive homes, she was bemused. At around 3,000 square feet, her house is among the smallest — yet she said it’s where her neighborhood pals prefer to hang out. Courtesy of Preeti Shah Shah’s lounge area with convertible coffee-to-dining room table A design principle Shah prioritizes, in any sized space, is double duty. “Anything I purchase, I would like for my client to be able to use it in more than just one way,” she shared. Ottomans are great for seating and storage, twin beds can become kings when guests stay over, and dining chairs should be comfy enough to be used as additional living room seating. In her own house, rather than a dining room table that sits unused, she opted for a convertible coffee table that lifts and extends to seat 10. Size and Amount Matter Troitsky explained that getting furniture that’s sized correctly can help a lot with how large your home feels (e.g., an enormous couch in a tiny bedroom might make the space seem small). But that doesn’t mean you should automatically purchase miniature versions of everything you’d buy for a bigger area. “It’s best to take inventory of what you actually use, need, and love, and start there,” Navarro said. She added: “For holiday decor, instead of trying to deck out every inch of your small living space, pick one or two areas to really lean into — the Christmas tree, the mantel, the coffee table, etc.” Get Comfortable With Borrowing Why use up valuable storage space on extra glassware and guest seating for your one annual holiday get-together when you can call a friend and ask to borrow theirs? As a bonus, it gives you both an excuse for a visit. Another option is to rent what you need when you need it. Ultimately, do your best to remember that, as Navarro put it, “the goal is always to make your guests feel at home — not to impress them with how big your place is!” RELATED: Make Your Home Happier With These Dopamine-Inducing Decorating Tips

items.titleOriginal: Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students

Το στρατόπεδο βρίσκεται κοντά στο t…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. In March 2020, COVID lockdowns shuttered schools around the world, including at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, where Prince Bashangezi was completing his A-Level studies. The camp sits near the Mozambique border, home to more than 17,000 people displaced by conflict across central and eastern Africa. Formal schooling stopped. Prince and a group of fellow A-Level students at USAP Community School, a school serving refugee youth in the camp, decided not to wait for it to resume. They founded TWEENS : Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. The model was built around what they had: each other. Teaching from inside the camp TWEENS began as a service learning project, with refugee students tutoring younger students in the same camp. The premise was direct. These were students who understood exactly what it meant to study without resources, without stability , often without continuous access to teachers, and in many cases without families to support them. They knew the particular difficulty of trying to build a future from inside a displaced population. So they taught each other. The program was supported by Education Matters Africa , a Zimbabwe-based nonprofit, and launched at a moment when any alternative to organized education was better than none. What began during a global lockdown became something that outlasted it. Prince was also a Waterford Kamhlaba UWC of Southern Africa alumnus, a school known for selecting students across conflict zones and economic hardship who show unusual potential and commitment. That network eventually connected him to the Global Student Haven Initiative at Pomona College in California, where he now studies computer science and economics. Marianne Langridge, who nominated Prince for this series, wrote that he “has turned his personal tragedy of losing his family during war into loving service for others.” That framing, loss converted into something that benefits others, runs through how Prince has talked about his work and what TWEENS is for. Langridge described his commitment as rooted in wanting students in refugee camps to “gain access to education so they can have hope for a better future.” Why peer tutoring works here There is something specific about a peer model in a refugee context that a standard school or aid program can’t replicate. The tutors in TWEENS are not professionals, not volunteers flying in from outside, not people working from a comfortable distance. They are students who live where the students they’re teaching live. They went through the same disruptions. Their credibility comes from proximity, not credentials. This is similar in structure to the peer-learning model that makes other youth-run programs effective, but in a refugee camp the stakes of educational continuity are different. A child who falls significantly behind in a displacement context faces a compounding disadvantage. Keeping any educational thread alive, even an informal one built by A-Level students during a lockdown, matters more than it might in a setting with backup resources. TWEENS was built on that understanding. From Tongogara to Pomona Prince arrived at Pomona College through the Global Student Haven Initiative , which supports students from refugee and displaced communities. He is studying computer science and economics, a combination that maps directly to the problems TWEENS is trying to solve: how technology and resource allocation interact to either expand or cut off access to education. Pomona profiled him in 2024 as part of a piece on Global Haven students finding opportunity in higher education. A fundraising campaign on GlobalGiving continues to support TWEENS’ operations, keeping the peer tutoring program funded as he completes his degree. What Prince Bashangezi and his fellow students built during a lockdown in a refugee camp, with nothing but time and knowledge and the willingness to share both, is still running more than five years later. TWEENS now offers an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside its original peer tutoring. To support TWEENS, visit their GlobalGiving fundraising page . The post Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The question hanging over international climate talks for years has not really been whether the world would shift away from fossil fuels. It has been whether the countries most responsible for burning them would actually put that transition in writing, with a plan attached. On November 3, Brazil did exactly that, releasing what it calls the world’s first global roadmap for phasing out coal, oil and gas. The document doesn’t bind anyone. It’s voluntary, and it acknowledges upfront that countries will move at different speeds and need different kinds of support. It names the transition as “urgent, inevitable and yet possible” and lays out a three-phase agenda running from 2028 to 2033, during which countries are urged to start drawing up plans and transforming their energy systems. “Countries differ in how fast they can move and in the support they need,” it states, “but every country gains from immediately planning its transition away from fossil fuels.” Why COP30 ended without naming fossil fuels The COP30 climate summit, held earlier this year in Belém, ended without final text that explicitly named fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia, and other major oil producers pushed back against direct language. Fortunately, the Brazilian presidency didn’t treat that as a dead end. Instead, it spent the remaining months of its COP30 term putting together a voluntary framework that any country can use to plan its own phaseout, entirely separate from whatever gets negotiated at a formal summit. COP30 chief executive Ana Toni framed the roadmap in terms of self-interest as much as obligation. “The transition is inevitable, so start planning now and as soon as possible, because this will be good for your country, for your society, for your economy,” she said. Brazil also released a companion roadmap on halting deforestation by 2030. A three-phase transition plan, tailored by country The roadmap doesn’t tell anyone exactly what to do. It says outright that “there is no unique solution for this complex puzzle” and pushes countries to tailor their approach to their own circumstances and starting points. The framing throughout is that the transition is a logistics problem, something to start working on with tools and knowledge that already exist, not a debate to be settled at some future summit. COP30 president André Corrêa do Lago was blunt about it: “Everyone can start to act now. The agreements already exist. What’s important is to implement them.” The document also points out that current policies still leave the world short of the commitments made at COP28 in Dubai in 2023, when nearly 200 nations agreed to language about “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems.” Three years later, that language hasn’t moved much. The roadmap is an attempt to change that without waiting on another round of negotiations to get there. The roadmap’s role at COP31 in Antalya The COP31 conference opened in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9 with the roadmap on the agenda, though Brazil has been clear it’s not there for renegotiation. “We are not suggesting negotiations,” Corrêa do Lago said. It’s a standing offer. Turkey and Australia, which are co-steering this year’s talks, have put electrification at the center of COP31’s agenda as a path to cutting emissions. The concern critics have raised is a practical one: the draft text doesn’t specify clean sources, which leaves open the possibility that “electrification” gets used to describe fossil fuel expansion rather than a genuine move to renewables. How that plays out over the two weeks in Antalya will shape what the summit actually delivers. Climate advocates are pushing for specificity. “The roadmap must not end up as just another report gathering dust on a shelf,” said Fanny Petitbon, a policy analyst at 350.org. “COP31 must be the moment when governments take this work forward, with clear commitments, timelines and the resources to deliver a fair and orderly exit from coal, oil and gas.” The framing shift that may outlast any summit The roadmap has no legal teeth. However, what it does have is a particular assumption baked in, namely that the question isn’t whether the fossil fuel transition happens, but how. That’s a different starting point than the one that has dominated climate negotiations for most of the past decade, where the fight was still about whether countries would formally commit to leaving fossil fuels behind at all. Brazil’s document takes that commitment as a given and asks what planning for it looks like. Whether the summits that follow treat it that way remains to be seen, but the document is in the world now, and that changes what any country can point to when it decides to start. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.description: Η καλύτερη φωτογραφία σας κάνει να επιβραδύνετε και να παρατηρήσετε κάτι που διαφορετικά θα μπορούσε να αγνοηθεί — και οι φιναλίστ για την όγδοη έκδοση του Close-Up Photographer of the Year κάνουν ακριβώς αυτό. items.descriptionOriginal: The best photography makes you slow down and notice something that might otherwise go overlooked — and the finalists for the eighth edition of Close-Up Photographer of the Year do just that. The shortlisted images were just revealed out of a record 15,388 submissions across 11 categories. The above shot, titled “Golden dust,” is one of the contenders in the animals category and features a Eurasian hoopoe taking a dust bath outside of Aurangabad, India. The dust helps remove excess oil from the bird’s feathers so they don’t stick together, but according to photographer Sarthak Agrawal, the swirling particles also make a good shot “especially difficult” (and thus especially impressive). “This year’s shortlist is a fabulous showcase of imagination, technical expertise, and natural curiosity,” competition co-founder Tracy Calder said in a press release shared with Nice News. The top 100 pics and the winning photographers will be announced in January, but submissions aren’t closed just yet. The competition holds an adjacent challenge that follows a specific theme, and this year’s is “Close to Home.” Hopeful shutterbugs of any age and skill level have until Nov. 30 to enter and Dec. 7 to upload their pics to the website. “Proving you don’t have to travel far to find something extraordinary,” the website states about the theme choice, which was voted on by the public. “We’re looking for close-up, macro, and micro photographs taken in a home and its immediate surroundings: the home’s rooms, outbuildings (such as sheds, garages, and greenhouses), garden, balcony, doorstep, or the street directly outside. This may be your own home or the home of family or friends.” Scroll to view a selection of the shortlisted images. Studio Art: “Rose Thorns” by Donald Bolak © Donald Bolak/CUPOTY “Fairly high level of magnification for a macro shot of a single rose thorn. The larger thorn is about 3/8 inch high. This is one of the things I enjoy most about macro — discovering sights unseen and unimagined. In this case a slightly surreal and alien landscape where rose thorns can be mountain peaks.” Young: “A Little Punky” by Oliver Lacey © Oliver Lacey/CUPOTY “I photographed this male Green Jumping Spider (Mopsus mormon) with its characteristic (and rather impressive) mohawk hairstyle in my suburban backyard in Brisbane, Australia.” Invertebrate Portrait: “Isopod portrait” by Adam Ferry © Adam Ferry/CUPOTY “I found this woodlouse resting underneath a piece of bark in a local woodland in Surrey, England. As it was fairly cold the woodlouse remained perfectly still allowing me to capture this focus stack of 80 photos. I love the high level of detail I could due to the increased magnification as the portrait filled most of the frame.” Underwater: “Rockpool Sanctuary” by Lisa Skelton © Lisa Skelton/CUPOTY “Young elephant seal pups or ‘weaners’ gather around natural rock pools on the Falkland Islands, using the protected waters to practice swimming and diving until they are ready to venture out to sea.” Intimate Landscape: “Where Worlds Collide” by Johannes Kowalewski © Johannes Kowalewski/CUPOTY “High above the Baltic Sea, an ancient beech forest glows in autumn colorrs atop the dramatic white chalk cliffs of Jasmund National Park on the island of Rügen, Germany.” Animals: “Nosepick” by Steffen Foerster © Steffen Foerster/CUPOTY “A blackish cinclodes or tussock-bird (Cinclodes antarcticus) picks at the nose of a resting southern elephant seal (Mirounga leonina) on Sea Lion Island, in the Falkland Islands.” Insects: “Spoonwing” by Lucien Harris © Lucien Harris/CUPOTY “I followed this spoonwing for over 10 minutes as it clumsily flew along the border of an overgrown field in the Peloponnese region of Greece, waiting for the perfect backdrop to compose a photo of this beautiful creature.” Underwater: “Fish Out of Context” by Marco Domenicucci © Marco Domenicucci/CUPOTY “A shoal of goldfish swim in an urban pond inside a metropolitan business district. Two worlds divided by a thin waterline: glass and concrete above and an aquatic ecosystem below.” Young: “Fight for the Perfect Fishing Spot” by Sasha Jumanca © Sasha Jumanca/CUPOTY “I managed to photograph these two blue kingfishers in December while they were defending their fishing territory in Schlosspark Nymphenburger, Munich. They faced each other directly and even tried to push one another under the water, showing how they compete for the best spots. This kind of behavior is quite rare, as kingfishers usually defend their territory by calling or chasing each other, rather than through physical contact.” Intimate Landscape: “Untitled 14” by Lukas Furlan © Lukas Furlan/CUPOTY “I was already fascinated by this scene, but rotating the image later revealed an entirely different world, almost like looking through a portal. It’s a reminder of the magic of experimentation and unexpected discoveries in photography.” Animals: “Suspended” by Joao Pontes © Joao Pontes/CUPOTY “In Portugal, there is no reptile quite as remarkable as the chameleon. Every year, towards the end of summer, the Algarve fills with juvenile chameleons. Naturally discreet, they become more active as the sun climbs higher in the sky, setting off to explore the world around them. Here, at the edge of the ocean, they inhabit the coastal dunes. At their scale, the slender stems of sea pinks become towering lianas, suspended pathways through this sandy jungle. To capture this image, I used a fisheye lens, aiming for a composition that would reveal not only the chameleon itself, but also the perhaps unexpected habitat it calls home.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Going digital is often assumed to be a modern, efficient strategy that will save energy and resources: picture smart cities and industries humming along, with everything needed to run them stored cleanly in the cloud. The reality is just the opposite, according to a new study. Across 20 of the world’s largest economies, the growth of information technology has increased environmental burdens—largely because of the energy required to build and run digital infrastructure . In the new study, researchers gathered World Bank data on the G20 economies from 1990 through 2023. This group of large economies accounts for 80% of global GDP and 70% of carbon emissions. The researchers looked at three indicators of digitalization: internet usage, landline telephone subscriptions, and cellular subscriptions. They used a variety of statistical techniques to probe the direct and indirect associations between these indicators and carbon emissions. Past studies have established that information and communications technologies have yielded huge social and economic benefits for nations around the world, but the environmental consequences of these technologies have been less clear. All three indicators of digitalization are associated with higher carbon emissions, the researchers found. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , .IRPP_ruby:visited , .IRPP_ruby:active {border:0!important;}.IRPP_ruby .clearfix:after {content: "";display: table;clear: both;}.IRPP_ruby {display: block;transition: background-color 250ms;webkit-transition: background-color 250ms;width: 100%;opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: #eaeaea;}.IRPP_ruby:active , .IRPP_ruby:hover {opacity: 1;transition: opacity 250ms;webkit-transition: opacity 250ms;background-color: inherit;}.IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl {background-position: center;background-size: cover;float: left;margin: 0;padding: 0;width: 31.59%;position: absolute;top: 0;bottom: 0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {float: right;width: 65.65%;padding:0;margin:0;}.IRPP_ruby .centered-text {display: table;height: 130px;left: 0;top: 0;padding:0;margin:0;padding-top: 20px;padding-bottom: 20px;}.IRPP_ruby .IRPP_ruby-content {display: table-cell;margin: 0;padding: 0 74px 0 0px;position: relative;vertical-align: middle;width: 100%;}.IRPP_ruby .ctaText {border-bottom: 0 solid #fff;color: #0099cc;font-size: 14px;font-weight: bold;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .postTitle {color: #000000;font-size: 16px;font-weight: 600;letter-spacing: normal;margin: 0;padding: 0;font-family:'Arial';}.IRPP_ruby .ctaButton {background: url(https://www.anthropocenemagazine.org/wp-content/plugins/intelly-related-posts-pro/assets/images/next-arrow.png)no-repeat;background-color: #afb4b6;background-position: center;display: inline-block;height: 100%;width: 54px;margin-left: 10px;position: absolute;bottom:0;right: 0;top: 0;}.IRPP_ruby:after {content: "";display: block;clear: both;} Recommended Reading: The average Internet user spends 3,230 hours online every year. Here's the carbon footprint of that. Strikingly, this pattern was almost entirely due to direct effects—that is, the energy needed to build and power digital infrastructure. “Data centers, device connectivity, and communication networks consume significant amounts of energy, which is largely sourced from carbon-intensive electricity,” the researchers write. The results suggest that the environmental benefits of digitalization depend on green electricity to power it—and at a global scale, that shift largely hasn’t happened yet. Clean energy is well known to be a key factor in determining the environmental benefits of electric cars . That relationship might not be as obvious in the case of digital technologies—it’s easy to overlook the energy required to make bits and bytes go bopping around the planet—but it’s no less crucial, the new work shows. The researchers expected that the early stages of digitalization, such as land line phone use, would be associated with increasing environmental burden but later stages, represented by internet and cellular adoption, with reduced carbon emissions—a pattern known as an environmental Kuznets curve. “In fact, economic and digital expansion continue to increase emissions rather than reduce them in the G20, revealing that these economies prioritize higher production and income over the cleaner environmental trajectory they often claim to pursue,” the researchers write. The upshot is that a push for digitalization needs to be accompanied by an effort to decarbonize the electricity that powers digital technologies, the researchers argue. Going forward, they say, governments should evaluate digitalization efforts not just in terms of technology access but also in terms of their climate impacts. Source: Alabdulwahab S. et al. “ ICT and CO2 Emissions in the G20: A Channel-Based Mediation Analysis .” Sustainability 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine
